title: Time Running Backwards, and Where It Stops: Superoscillations of Proper Time and the Memory of the Environment
comment: 18 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Ancillary files: code for the exact two-branch calculation and Fig. 3
summary: A quantum system prepared in a superposition of proper times - a clock whose worldline is superposed, or a clock at rest in a superposed gravitational potential - evolves, in each branch, by the same dynamics for a different duration. Post-selecting the control that sets the proper time turns the superposition into a superoscillation of the time-dilation factor: the system is found to have evolved for a proper time $α_w t$, where the weak value $α_w$ may exceed unity, vanish, or be negative - the quantum time-translation machine of Aharonov, Anandan, Popescu and Vaidman. We ask how far back such a machine can run an irreversible process. The test system is a sealed cell - excited atoms, the radiation field they emit into, and the absorbing walls, carried as one quantum object - and the witness is projective: atoms that had begun to decay before the run are found, in the post-selected sub-ensemble, more excited than when inserted. The answer is exact and depends only on the atoms' survival amplitude. With two branches the witness holds only while the decay is younger than the memory time of the environment, after which the emission becomes Markovian. Beyond it, the post-selection amplifies the minute difference between the contents of the cell in the two branches, set by the full energy spread of the atoms and their field rather than by the linewidth, and the witness fails. Reversing a decay past the memory time requires many branches, an environment with a strictly bounded spectrum, and a post-selection probability that falls exponentially with the number of environmental oscillations to be undone. The obstacle to reversal is therefore not entropy but bandwidth - the same bandwidth that makes the emission irreversible in the first place. We give four ways to superpose a clock rate, from hollow massive shells to inertial velocities.

AI.tldr: The paper asks how far a "quantum time-translation machine" (a superoscillating time-dilation factor α_w via post-selection of a superposed proper time) can reverse an irreversible atomic decay, treated together with its emitted radiation field and absorbing walls as one sealed quantum object.
AI.motivation: A superposed proper time, post-selected, yields a weak value α_w that can exceed unity, vanish, or be negative — the Aharonov–Anandan–Popescu–Vaidman time-translation machine. The authors want to determine how far such a machine can run an irreversible process (spontaneous decay) backward, and what fundamentally limits this reversal.
AI.method: The test system is a sealed cell consisting of excited atoms, the radiation field they emit into, and the absorbing walls, carried as a single quantum object. The witness is projective: in the post-selected sub-ensemble, atoms that had already begun to decay are found more excited than when inserted. The analysis is exact and depends only on the atoms' survival amplitude; two-branch superpositions are contrasted with multi-branch schemes, and four concrete ways to superpose a clock rate (from hollow massive shells to inertial velocities) are provided.
AI.result: With two branches, the witness holds only while the decay is younger than the memory (non-Markovian) time of the environment; beyond that the emission becomes Markovian and the witness fails. Past the memory time, post-selection only amplifies the minute branch difference set by the full energy spread of atoms and field (not the linewidth). Reversing decay beyond the memory time requires many branches, a strictly bounded environmental spectrum, and a post-selection probability falling exponentially with the number of environmental oscillations to be undone.
AI.conclusion: The fundamental obstacle to reversing an irreversible decay is not entropy but bandwidth — the same bandwidth that makes the emission irreversible in the first place.

title: Second-level termination of the PPT entanglement-cost hierarchy for two qutrits
summary: We prove that for arbitrary two-qutrit quantum states, the semidefinite programming lower-bound hierarchy for the PPT entanglement cost terminates at the second level. Therefore, under operations preserving positive partial transpose, its zero-error asymptotic entanglement cost can be obtained by a semidefinite program involving only three Hermitian matrix variables. The key to the proof is to shorten the feasible dual chain by one level; to this end, we combine finite certificates verified by exact rational arithmetic with analytic estimates near the boundary of the parameter domain. This result shows that a unified terminating level exists for two-qutrit systems, whereas no unified terminating level exists for all dimensions.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that the semidefinite programming (SDP) lower-bound hierarchy for the PPT entanglement cost of arbitrary two-qutrit states terminates at the second level, yielding a three-variable SDP for the zero-error asymptotic entanglement cost under PPT-preserving operations.
AI.motivation: The SDP lower-bound hierarchy for PPT entanglement cost is infinite in general, and no unified terminating level exists across all dimensions. Whether a finite, uniform termination level exists for two-qutrit systems was open; establishing it would make the cost computable via a small SDP.
AI.method: Prove termination at level two by shortening the feasible dual chain by one level. Combine finite certificates verified with exact rational arithmetic together with analytic estimates near the boundary of the parameter domain.
AI.result: For arbitrary two-qutrit states, the hierarchy terminates at the second level, so the zero-error asymptotic entanglement cost under PPT-preserving operations is given by an SDP with only three Hermitian matrix variables. A unified terminating level exists for two-qutrit systems, in contrast to the general all-dimensions case.
AI.conclusion: Two-qutrit PPT entanglement cost admits a finite-level (level-two) SDP characterization, establishing dimension-specific uniform termination of the hierarchy.

title: Quantum simulation of real-time bosonic dynamics with binary and unary position encodings on superconducting and trapped-ion processors
summary: Simulating a bosonic degree of freedom on qubit hardware requires discretizing its position space, and the qubit encoding of the resulting lattice determines the circuits that realize its real-time dynamics. We compare binary and unary encodings of a position lattice on superconducting (IBM) and trapped-ion (IonQ) processors. Binary encoding applies the kinetic term through the quantum Fourier transform; unary encoding uses one qubit per site, single-qubit rotations for the potential and excitation-conserving exchange gates for the kinetic term. For a single degree of freedom the unary dynamics is a free-fermion problem, and its product formula compresses exactly into a nearest-neighbor circuit of fixed size. With about two hundred two-qubit gates, these circuits resolve tunneling in a symmetric double well on both processors, with the right-well probability falling from 0.97 to 0.06 on IBM and from 0.96 to 0.12 on IonQ, whereas binary product-formula circuits with several thousand two-qubit gates do not reproduce the transfer. Noiseless emulation indicates that this contrast reflects the compilation as well as the encoding: without the fixed-size optimization, a unary product formula that captures the transfer also requires several thousand two-qubit gates. Post-selection on the single-excitation subspace removes leakage, and because every energy eigenstate of the symmetric grid populates both wells equally, the measured population reversal bounds the coherence between energy eigenstates from below. Coupled-oscillator benchmarks, where inter-register interactions prevent this exact compression, show that the preferred encoding depends on the grid size and the evolution time.

AI.tldr: The paper compares binary and unary qubit encodings of a discretized bosonic position lattice on IBM superconducting and IonQ trapped-ion hardware, showing that unary encoding with exact circuit compression resolves double-well tunneling using ~200 two-qubit gates while binary encoding requires several thousand and fails to reproduce the transfer.
AI.motivation: Simulating bosonic degrees of freedom on qubit hardware requires discretizing position space, and the choice of qubit encoding determines the circuits realizing real-time dynamics. The paper asks which encoding (binary vs. unary) is preferable in practice on current quantum processors.
AI.method: Binary encoding implements the kinetic term via the quantum Fourier transform; unary encoding uses one qubit per site with single-qubit rotations for the potential and excitation-conserving exchange gates for the kinetic term. For a single degree of freedom, the unary dynamics is a free-fermion problem whose product formula compresses exactly into a fixed-size nearest-neighbor circuit. Experiments run on IBM (superconducting) and IonQ (trapped-ion) processors; post-selection on the single-excitation subspace removes leakage, and population reversal is used to lower-bound coherence between energy eigenstates. Coupled-oscillator benchmarks probe the regime where exact compression fails.
AI.result: With about two hundred two-qubit gates, unary circuits resolve tunneling in a symmetric double well on both processors: the right-well probability falls from 0.97 to 0.06 on IBM and from 0.96 to 0.12 on IonQ. In contrast, binary product-formula circuits with several thousand two-qubit gates do not reproduce the transfer. Noiseless emulation shows this contrast stems from compilation as well as encoding: without the fixed-size optimization, a unary product formula capturing the transfer also needs several thousand two-qubit gates. Coupled-oscillator benchmarks show the preferred encoding depends on grid size and evolution time.
AI.conclusion: The unary encoding with exact circuit compression is far more gate-efficient for single bosonic degrees of freedom and enables tunneling experiments on current hardware, whereas the binary approach is impractical at comparable fidelity. Since inter-register interactions prevent exact compression, the optimal encoding is problem-dependent, governed by grid size and evolution time.

title: Field-induced phase-matching in Josephson traveling wave parametric amplifiers
summary: Superconducting Josephson traveling wave parametric amplifiers (JTWPAs) enable broadband, quantum-limited amplification of weak microwave signals. JTWPAs are essential for the single-shot readout of superconducting qubits, broadband vacuum squeezing, or the generation of microwave cluster states. Phase-matching between signal and pump modes in such JTWPAs represents a major engineering challenge, which is typically solved by integrating resonators in a nonlinear medium in order to tailor electromagnetic dispersion relations and achieve a broadband, high-gain amplification. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a phase-matching approach using a homogeneous nonlinear medium based on Josephson elements by exploiting a magnetic field inhomogeneity. We show how the latter may lead to the sign reversal of the 3-wave mixing nonlinearity and stabilization of the parametric amplification. We envision this technique as a viable alternative to conventional phase-matching approaches.

AI.tldr: A homogeneous Josephson-element nonlinear medium achieves phase matching for Josephson traveling wave parametric amplification by exploiting a magnetic field inhomogeneity that reverses the sign of 3-wave-mixing nonlinearity and stabilizes parametric gain.
AI.motivation: JTWPAs provide broadband quantum-limited microwave amplification for single-shot qubit readout, vacuum squeezing, and microwave cluster-state generation, but phase matching between signal and pump modes is a major engineering challenge, conventionally solved by embedding resonators in the nonlinear medium to engineer dispersion.
AI.method: Instead of resonator-based dispersion engineering, the authors use a homogeneous nonlinear medium built from Josephson elements and exploit a magnetic field inhomogeneity, showing that it can induce a sign reversal of the 3-wave-mixing nonlinearity and stabilize the parametric amplification.
AI.result: Experimental demonstration of phase matching in a homogeneous Josephson-element medium via magnetic field inhomogeneity, with sign reversal of the 3WM nonlinearity and stabilized parametric amplification.
AI.conclusion: Magnetic-field-inhomogeneity-based phase matching is proposed as a viable alternative to conventional resonator-based dispersion-engineering approaches for JTWPAs.

title: Spin-glass order in a field requires magnetic-field chaos in XY gauge glasses for $d\leq 4$
summary: The XY gauge-glass model is believed to exhibit a spin-glass phase in dimensions $d\geq 3$. In this paper, we prove that, in dimensions $d\leq 4$ and at any finite temperature, a magnetic field applied in a fixed direction, with amplitudes that fluctuate from site to site according to the Rayleigh distribution, must either induce magnetic-field chaos in the spin-glass phase or destroy spin-glass order altogether, whenever a spin-glass phase exists at zero field. In particular, if a spin-glass phase persists under such a field, as predicted by the replica-symmetry-breaking (RSB) picture, it must exhibit magnetic-field chaos. This conclusion follows from our proof that, for any fixed nonzero field strength, the disorder average of the squared overlap between equilibrium spin configurations at zero field and those at nonzero field vanishes in the thermodynamic limit. By gauge transformations, the overlap statistics are identical to the magnetization statistics of an XY gauge glass with correlated bond disorder in a Gaussian random field. Our proof combines this exact identity with quantitative estimates on the suppression of ferromagnetic order by random fields in continuous-spin systems, due to Dario, Harel, and Peled [Commun. Math. Phys. 405, 212 (2024)] and building on the work of Imry and Ma [Phys. Rev. Lett. 35, 1399 (1975)] and of Aizenman and Wehr [Phys. Rev. Lett. 62, 2503 (1989); Commun. Math. Phys. 130, 489 (1990)]. We extend these estimates to bond-dependent interactions. Although our result provides a rare rigorous constraint on the nature of spin-glass phases in finite-dimensional systems, it does not determine whether spin-glass order survives in a field, and therefore does not distinguish between the droplet and RSB pictures. The case of a strictly uniform field remains open.

AI.tldr: In dimensions d ≤ 4, a random-direction Rayleigh-distributed magnetic field either destroys spin-glass order or forces it to exhibit magnetic-field chaos; if spin-glass order survives such a field (as RSB predicts), magnetic-field chaos is inevitable.
AI.motivation: The XY gauge-glass model is believed to have a spin-glass phase in d ≥ 3, but rigorous constraints on the nature of spin-glass phases in finite dimensions are scarce. The authors aim to establish whether an applied random magnetic field is compatible with spin-glass order and whether it induces magnetic-field chaos.
AI.method: They prove that, for any fixed nonzero field strength, the disorder average of the squared overlap between zero-field and nonzero-field equilibrium spin configurations vanishes in the thermodynamic limit. Via gauge transformations, the overlap statistics are mapped exactly onto the magnetization statistics of an XY gauge glass with correlated bond disorder in a Gaussian random field. They then combine this identity with quantitative estimates on random-field suppression of ferromagnetic order (Dario–Harel–Peled, building on Imry–Ma and Aizenman–Wehr), extended here to bond-dependent interactions.
AI.result: In d ≤ 4 and at any finite temperature, a fixed-direction field with site-to-site Rayleigh-distributed amplitudes must either induce magnetic-field chaos in the spin-glass phase or destroy spin-glass order entirely, whenever zero-field spin-glass order exists. In particular, if a spin-glass phase persists under such a field, RSB predicts it must exhibit magnetic-field chaos.
AI.conclusion: The result provides a rare rigorous constraint on spin-glass phases in finite-dimensional systems but does not determine whether spin-glass order survives in a field, and hence does not distinguish droplet from RSB pictures. The strictly uniform-field case remains open.

title: Time Direction Entanglement Entropy of Free Fermion Ground States
summary: While the entanglement entropy of a spatial subregion has been extensively studied, a properly defined entanglement entropy of quantum states in a time direction interval remains underexplored. We investigate the scaling behaviors of the recently defined time direction entanglement entropy (TDEE) for free fermion quantum states, which is computed from the reduced density matrix of a sub-Hilbert space that minimally supports all the time-evolved operators in the time direction interval. Based on the Fisher--Hartwig conjecture for Toeplitz matrices, we develop an analytical framework for understanding the TDEE in a time interval with discrete time step $τ$. For disorderless one-dimensional (1D) systems (gapless fermions or band insulators), in different regimes of gap, bandwidth and $τ$, we find the TDEE can exhibit area law (for nonzero gap), logarithmic law or volume law in the length of time. For 1D Anderson insulators, we numerically find the TDEE shows a Page-curve like behavior, growing at short time, and decaying in power-law at long time exceeding the crossover time determined by localization. In the continuum time limit $τ\rightarrow 0$, the TDEE of disorderless gapless fermions, band insulators and Anderson insulators exhibit logarithmic law, area law and sub-area law, respectively. We also show that the sub-Hilbert space of a time-direction interval stabilizes in the $τ\rightarrow 0$ limit, which is understandable as a subspace of the Hilbert space of the Lieb-Robinson causal diamond.

AI.tldr: This paper analytically and numerically studies the time direction entanglement entropy (TDEE) of free fermion states, showing it exhibits area, logarithmic, or volume-law scaling in time depending on gap, bandwidth, disorder, and discrete time step.
AI.motivation: Entanglement entropy of spatial subregions is well studied, but a properly defined entanglement entropy for quantum states along a time-direction interval remains underexplored.
AI.method: TDEE is computed from the reduced density matrix of the minimal sub-Hilbert space supporting all time-evolved operators in a time interval. An analytical framework based on the Fisher–Hartwig conjecture for Toeplitz matrices is developed for discrete time step τ, complemented by numerical study of 1D Anderson insulators.
AI.result: For disorderless 1D systems (gapless fermions and band insulators), TDEE exhibits area law (nonzero gap), logarithmic law, or volume law in time length across regimes of gap, bandwidth, and τ. For 1D Anderson insulators, TDEE shows a Page-curve-like behavior: growth at short times and power-law decay beyond a localization-determined crossover. In the τ→0 limit, disorderless gapless fermions, band insulators, and Anderson insulators show logarithmic, area, and sub-area laws respectively.
AI.conclusion: The sub-Hilbert space of a time-direction interval stabilizes in the τ→0 limit and is interpretable as a subspace of the Hilbert space of the Lieb–Robinson causal diamond.

title: Disorder-Induced Logarithmic Spreading and Localization of Quantum Fluctuations
summary: Disorder can localize quantum particles, even in the presence of interactions, but its influence on quantum fluctuations beyond mean--field dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the propagation of quantum fluctuations in weakly interacting disordered bosonic systems by comparing the Bose--Hubbard model with the Gross--Pitaevskii equation. We find that, in contrast to ballistic spreading in the disorder--free system, quantum fluctuations exhibit logarithmic spreading at intermediate times under both random and quasiperiodic disorder, before eventually saturating. The spreading rate decreases algebraically with increasing disorder strength, and this behavior persists across different particle numbers and extends to two dimensions. Using a time--dependent Bogoliubov--de Gennes framework, we identify the localized mean--field wavefunction as a time--dependent pairing background that generates quantum fluctuations. The exponential suppression of fluctuation--generation rates with distance provides a physical mechanism for the logarithmically advancing fluctuation front. Our results reveal a distinct regime of disorder--controlled quantum--fluctuation dynamics and establish disorder as a means of controlling their spreading.

AI.tldr: Quantum fluctuations in weakly interacting disordered bosonic systems spread logarithmically in time (rather than ballistically), with a rate that decays algebraically with disorder strength, before saturating.
AI.motivation: Disorder is known to localize quantum particles even with interactions, but its effect on quantum fluctuations beyond mean-field dynamics is poorly understood. The authors aim to characterize how fluctuations propagate in weakly interacting disordered bosonic systems.
AI.method: Compare the Bose–Hubbard model with the Gross–Pitaevskii equation for weakly interacting bosons under random and quasiperiodic disorder. Use a time-dependent Bogoliubov–de Gennes framework to connect fluctuation generation to the localized mean-field wavefunction acting as a time-dependent pairing background.
AI.result: In contrast to ballistic spreading in the disorder-free case, fluctuations show logarithmic spreading at intermediate times under both random and quasiperiodic disorder, eventually saturating. The spreading rate decreases algebraically with disorder strength, is robust across particle numbers, and extends to two dimensions. The exponential suppression of fluctuation-generation rates with distance explains the logarithmically advancing front.
AI.conclusion: The work identifies a distinct regime of disorder-controlled quantum-fluctuation dynamics and establishes disorder as a tool for controlling fluctuation spreading.

title: Kinematic Quantum Geometry
summary: Kinematic quantum geometry describes fast degrees of freedom (DOFs) that adiabatically follow states parametrized by both the coordinates and the velocities of slow DOFs. It extends Born-Oppenheimer geometry, which depends on coordinates alone, introduces mixed Berry curvatures, and modifies the effective theory governing the slow DOFs. We test its predictions in two setups: spinful particles moving in magnetic textures, and Dirac electrons in graphene coupled to an LC circuit. In the first, kinematic quantum geometry produces a velocity-dependent effective mass tensor and generates a Lorentz-like force nonlinear in velocity that can arise even in coplanar textures. In the second, it renormalizes the circuit capacitance and generates a Hall current nonlinear in the electric field. For small velocities, it reproduces recent results for electronic dynamics in external electromagnetic fields and in pseudospin textures. However, the framework can remain valid at large velocities beyond the perturbative regime, provided the kinematic states are sufficiently slowly varying.

AI.tldr: The paper develops "kinematic quantum geometry," which extends Born-Oppenheimer geometry (coordinate-only) to cases where fast DOFs adiabatically track states depending on both coordinates and velocities of slow DOFs, producing mixed Berry curvatures that modify the slow-DOF effective theory. Two testbeds confirm predictions: velocity-dependent effective mass and a nonlinear Lorentz-like force in magnetic textures, and capacitance renormalization plus a nonlinear Hall current in graphene coupled to an LC circuit.
AI.motivation: Standard Born-Oppenheimer quantum geometry depends on slow coordinates alone and cannot capture fast DOFs that adiabatically follow states parametrized also by slow velocities. A framework is needed to describe the resulting mixed Berry curvatures and their corrections to the effective theory of slow DOFs.
AI.method: The authors formulate kinematic quantum geometry with mixed Berry curvatures and apply it to two setups: (1) spinful particles moving in magnetic textures, and (2) Dirac electrons in graphene coupled to an LC circuit. In each, they derive the emergent corrections (effective mass tensor, Lorentz-like force; capacitance renormalization, Hall current) and compare the small-velocity limit with existing results.
AI.result: Setup 1 yields a velocity-dependent effective mass tensor and a Lorentz-like force nonlinear in velocity, which arises even in coplanar textures. Setup 2 yields a renormalized circuit capacitance and a Hall current nonlinear in the electric field. The small-velocity limit reproduces recent results for electronic dynamics in external electromagnetic fields and in pseudospin textures.
AI.conclusion: Kinematic quantum geometry generalizes Born-Oppenheimer geometry and nonperturbatively modifies slow-DOF dynamics. Beyond reproducing known perturbative results, it remains valid at large velocities provided the kinematic states vary sufficiently slowly.

title: Surface codes with coherent errors: optimal decoding and finite-size crossovers
summary: We study the surface code under uniform coherent $Z$ rotations $\exp{(iθZ)}$ followed by perfect syndrome measurements, a setting known to exhibit strong finite-size effects that complicate the extraction of the asymptotic decoding threshold. We identify finite-size behavior of both Pauli decoding measures and the coherent information with two characteristic lengths: an algebraic ballistic-crossover scale $d_{\mathrm{ba}}\sim 1/β_R^α$ ($α=1$ for odd $d$ and $α=2$ for even $d$) and a much larger renormalization-group scale $d_\mathrm{RG}\sim \exp{(C/β^{4}_R)}$, where $β_R=-\tfrac{1}{2}\ln\tanθ$ and $d$ is the system size. As $θ$ approaches the ballistic SWAP point $π/4$, the two length scales diverge at very different rates, leaving a broad intermediate regime $d_{\mathrm{ba}}\ll d\ll d_\mathrm{RG}$ in which these quantities show substantial finite-size drift and approximate plateaus. To establish the microscopic basis of this crossover picture, we derive a leading inter-flavor quartic interaction of order $β_R^2$ in the replicated Majorana theory, which provides a route to the class-D nonlinear sigma model. The resulting marginal RG flow motivates the scaling variable $X_4=β_R^4\ln d$, in which free-fermion simulations show approximate collapse of decoding measures. These results are consistent with a Pauli-decoding threshold at $θ_c=π/4$ in the thermodynamic limit. For any even $d$, we prove that maximum-likelihood Pauli decoding maximizes entanglement fidelity over all deterministic syndrome-conditioned quantum recoveries, and that its decoding threshold attains the quantum-optimal limit, coinciding with the one defined by coherent information.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes finite-size scaling of the surface code under uniform coherent Z rotations followed by ideal syndrome measurements, identifying two distinct characteristic length scales (a ballistic crossover scale and a much larger RG scale) and connecting them via a replicated Majorana theory with an inter-flavor quartic interaction, while proving optimality of maximum-likelihood Pauli decoding.
AI.motivation: The coherent-error surface code exhibits strong finite-size effects that obscure extraction of the asymptotic decoding threshold, so a clear understanding of the crossover scales and their microscopic origin is needed.
AI.method: Identifies finite-size behavior through two length scales—ballistic crossover d_ba ~ 1/β_R^α and RG scale d_RG ~ exp(C/β_R^4)—derives a leading inter-flavor quartic interaction of order β_R^2 in the replicated Majorana theory (route to class-D nonlinear sigma model), and motivates the scaling variable X_4 = β_R^4 ln d; uses free-fermion simulations. Also proves maximum-likelihood Pauli decoding maximizes entanglement fidelity over all deterministic syndrome-conditioned recoveries for even d.
AI.result: A broad intermediate regime d_ba << d << d_RG exhibits substantial finite-size drift and approximate plateaus; scaling variable X_4 shows approximate collapse of decoding measures. ML Pauli decoding is proven optimal for entanglement fidelity and attains the quantum-optimal threshold coinciding with the coherent-information threshold.
AI.conclusion: Results are consistent with a Pauli-decoding threshold at θ_c = π/4 in the thermodynamic limit, and ML Pauli decoding achieves the quantum-optimal decoding limit for even d.

title: Frustration-free control for quantum-state preparation: an exact first-passage theory
summary: Quantum circuits based on local measurements and feedback can autonomously prepare and stabilize entangled many-body states. In frustration-free control, the target manifold is specified by local constraints, whose violations are detected by measurement and removed by feedback. We develop an exact theory of this mechanism for the preparation of Dicke states of $N_q$ qubits. Dicke states span the permutation-symmetric subspace, one per magnetization sector. Local singlet projectors define the constraints and detect departures from permutation symmetry. The resulting dynamics closes exactly on the span of the $N_q(N_q-1)/2$ singlet-pair projectors and is equivalent to a classical first-passage process: measurements move the pair endpoints, while feedback absorbs pairs on measured bonds. The closure reduces the exponentially large many-body Liouvillian to a generator of polynomial size. In one dimension we solve this process in closed form. Its slowest rate, $2[1-\cos(π/N_q)]$ in units of the measurement rate, is an exact Liouvillian eigenvalue. For any scheme of this class, the relaxation time is bounded below by the inverse fraction of pair configurations on which feedback acts; local feedback reaches $O(N_q)$ of $O(N_q^2)$ configurations, requiring a time at least linear in $N_q$. A second exact closure determines the final state reached from any initial condition. Extensions to modified transport, restricted feedback, and physical errors yield an exact transport-to-absorber crossover, geometric preparation laws, and a bound on the stationary leakage. An exact second-moment closure determines the ensemble fluctuations: the measurement noise is conserving, while feedback generates removal shot noise and pair correlations. Preparation, acceleration, robustness, and fluctuations are thus governed by one exactly solvable process: the transport and absorption of local constraint violations.

AI.tldr: An exact theory of measurement-and-feedback preparation of Dicke states is developed by showing that the many-body dynamics closes onto a polynomially sized space of singlet-pair projectors, reducing state preparation, its slowest relaxation rate, robustness, and fluctuations to one solvable classical transport-and-absorption process.
AI.motivation: Frustration-free control with local measurements and feedback can autonomously stabilize entangled many-body states, but a quantitative, exact understanding of the underlying preparation mechanism—its timescales, steady states, and noise—is lacking.
AI.method: Local singlet projectors are used as constraints that detect departures from permutation symmetry. The authors prove an exact closure of the Liouvillian onto the span of the N_q(N_q-1)/2 singlet-pair projectors, mapping the dynamics to a classical first-passage process where measurement moves pair endpoints and feedback absorbs pairs. They solve the 1D process in closed form, derive a general lower bound on relaxation time from the fraction of feedback-acted pair configurations, prove a second exact closure for the final state, and establish a second-moment closure for ensemble fluctuations.
AI.result: In 1D the slowest rate is exactly 2[1-cos(pi/N_q)] in measurement-rate units and is an exact Liouvillian eigenvalue. For any scheme in this class the relaxation time is bounded below by the inverse fraction of pair configurations where feedback acts; local feedback touches O(N_q) of O(N_q^2) configurations, implying at least linear-in-N_q time. Extensions yield an exact transport-to-absorber crossover, geometric preparation laws, and a bound on stationary leakage. The second-moment closure shows measurement noise is conserving while feedback generates removal shot noise and pair correlations.
AI.conclusion: Preparation, acceleration, robustness, and fluctuations of Dicke states are all governed by one exactly solvable process—the transport and absorption of local constraint violations—providing exact Liouvillian eigenvalues, fundamental speed limits, and quantitative error and noise predictions.

title: Third-Order Quantum Information from Distributed Randomized Measurements
summary: Randomized measurements offer a way to probe nonlinear properties of quantum states without reconstructing their full density matrices. For states shared between distant laboratories, we study products of three outcome probabilities measured at the same local settings and then averaged over independent local random unitaries. We determine, for an arbitrary number of parties, which third-order local-unitary invariant combinations these averages retain and which they cannot separate. The accessible information is encoded in algebraic invariants of the quantum state and is reconstructed by analysing the permutation symmetries induced by the distributed measurement protocol. Exploiting these symmetries, the reconstruction problem collapses, regardless of the number of measurement outcomes, to the symbolic inversion of a 3 x 3 matrix. As a result, nonlinear information can be extracted without inverting the exponentially large matrices that typically arise in distributed multipartite quantum systems.

AI.tldr: Third-order products of outcome probabilities averaged over independent local random unitaries yield a fixed set of local-unitary invariants whose reconstruction reduces to inverting a 3x3 matrix, independent of party number and outcome count.
AI.motivation: Probing nonlinear properties of quantum states shared across distant laboratories requires methods beyond full density-matrix reconstruction, which scales exponentially. The authors ask which third-order local-unitary invariants remain accessible under randomized measurements when outcome-probability products are averaged over independent local random unitaries.
AI.method: Products of three outcome probabilities are measured at identical local settings and averaged over independent local random unitaries, for an arbitrary number of parties. The accessible information is expressed as algebraic invariants of the state, and permutation symmetries induced by the distributed measurement protocol are analyzed to determine which invariant combinations are retained and which cannot be separated.
AI.result: The paper fully characterizes, for any number of parties, the third-order local-unitary invariant combinations that the averaged quantities retain and those they cannot distinguish. Exploiting the induced permutation symmetries, the reconstruction collapses—regardless of the number of measurement outcomes—to symbolic inversion of a 3x3 matrix.
AI.conclusion: Nonlinear information can be extracted from distributed multipartite states without inverting the exponentially large matrices typical of such systems, making the protocol scalable in both party number and local dimension.

title: Which data samples matter when training a quantum model?
summary: The expressivity, loss landscapes, and generalization behavior of quantum machine learning models have been studied extensively, yet mainly from a model-centric point of view. Little is known about the compatibility of particular quantum models with specific datasets. In this work, we study quantum machine learning models with a data-dependent focus by establishing a quantum-compatible form of the V-usable information. This metric quantifies the information a model can extract from a dataset, enabling a direct, data-centric comparison of different models. We employ this metric to study which data points contribute most significantly to a model's learning process. This enables us to develop an informed preselection strategy for data subsets that can significantly improve the data efficiency of the training pipeline. This work establishes the V-usable information as a powerful diagnostic tool for learning dynamics and a practical route to data-efficient quantum machine learning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a quantum-compatible form of V-usable information to measure, in a data-centric way, how much information a quantum model can extract from a dataset, and uses it to identify influential data points and preselect data subsets that improve data efficiency.
AI.motivation: Prior studies of expressivity, loss landscapes, and generalization in quantum machine learning are mostly model-centric; little is known about the compatibility between particular quantum models and specific datasets.
AI.method: The authors formulate a quantum-compatible variant of V-usable information, a metric quantifying the information a model can extract from a dataset, enabling direct data-centric comparison across models. They then apply the metric to assess which data points contribute most to learning, and derive a data-subset preselection strategy.
AI.result: The metric identifies which data points are most significant for a model's learning process, and the resulting preselection strategy yields significant improvements in data efficiency of the training pipeline.
AI.conclusion: V-usable information serves as a powerful diagnostic tool for learning dynamics and provides a practical route toward data-efficient quantum machine learning.

title: Finite Measured Entropy Production Does Not Imply Finite Microscopic Irreversibility
summary: Coarse-grained measurements provide a lower bound on entropy production, but how much microscopic irreversibility can they conceal? We construct a driven quantum system in which an imperfect counter registers a finite, strictly positive arrow of time while the microscopic entropy production is infinite. The system is a degenerate parametric oscillator below threshold, coupled to a thermal reservoir through repeated interactions with bosonic ancillas. The oscillator sustains a finite, positive heat current into the vacuum bath, where absorption is forbidden and forward and reverse trajectory laws have different supports. A photon counter with finite collection efficiency, gated time bins, and independent dark counts defines a common coarse-graining of the aligned trajectory laws. For fixed observation duration $\mathcal T$ and detector parameters, we prove that the observed relative entropy remains uniformly bounded as the bath temperature $T_b$ vanishes and is strictly positive at vacuum. The hidden contribution obeys $Σ_{\mathrm{hid}}(\mathcal T,T_b)=\mathcal T\dot Q_0/(k_BT_b)+O(1)$, where $\dot Q_0>0$ is the stationary vacuum heat current. False positives conceal the support mismatch while preserving measurable time asymmetry. Thus, finite and informative measurements of entropy production can coexist with infinite microscopic irreversibility.

AI.tldr: Coarse-grained measurements bound entropy production from below, but can conceal arbitrarily large microscopic irreversibility. The authors construct a driven quantum system—a degenerate parametric oscillator below threshold coupled to a thermal bath—where a realistic imperfect photon counter registers a finite, strictly positive arrow of time while the microscopic entropy production diverges. They prove the observed relative entropy stays uniformly bounded as bath temperature vanishes yet remains strictly positive at vacuum, with the hidden contribution scaling as 𝒯 Q̇₀/(k_B T_b).
AI.motivation: Coarse-grained observables give only a lower bound on entropy production, leaving open how much microscopic irreversibility they can hide. The paper asks whether a finite, informative time asymmetry—and a strictly positive arrow of time—can coexist with infinite microscopic entropy production under realistic (imperfect, lossy) measurement.
AI.method: A degenerate parametric oscillator below threshold is coupled to a thermal reservoir via repeated interactions with bosonic ancillas, sustaining a positive stationary heat current into a vacuum bath where absorption is forbidden, so forward and reverse trajectory laws have different supports. A photon counter with finite collection efficiency, gated time bins, and independent dark counts defines a common coarse-graining of the aligned trajectory laws; the observed relative entropy is analyzed as bath temperature T_b → 0 for fixed observation duration and detector parameters.
AI.result: For fixed observation duration 𝒯 and detector parameters, the observed relative entropy remains uniformly bounded as T_b → 0 and is strictly positive at vacuum. The hidden contribution obeys Σ_hid(𝒯, T_b) = 𝒯 Q̇₀/(k_B T_b) + O(1), with Q̇₀ > 0 the stationary vacuum heat current, so microscopic entropy production diverges while coarse-grained irreversibility stays finite.
AI.conclusion: Detector false positives (dark counts) conceal the support mismatch of the forward/reverse laws while preserving a measurable time asymmetry. Thus finite, informative measurements of entropy production can coexist with infinite microscopic irreversibility, showing coarse-grained bounds can drastically underestimate true dissipation.

title: FusionQ: A Generic and Optimal Decoding Framework for Ultra-Low-Latency Quantum Error Correction
summary: Quantum error correction (QEC) decoding has traditionally been organized around fixed decoding instances: a monolithic space-time detector error model (DEM), or a predetermined temporal window, is handed to a backend decoder after enough syndrome data has arrived. This paper presents FusionQ, a fusion decoding framework that changes this paradigm by deriving local decoding tasks from the observed syndrome and then fusing their results into a single global correction. Instead of forcing every shot through the same global or windowed problem, FusionQ builds open-boundary local DEMs around fired detector clusters and expands the corresponding footprints only when a local optimum uses virtual boundary errors. FusionQ is generic in the decoder backend: the scheduler requires only a local solution and a boundary-use flag, so exact solvers, matching-style decoders on graphlike DEMs, and heuristic decoders can share the same runtime. We prove a compositional optimality theorem: with an exact minimum-weight local backend and boundary-free publication, fusing the published local decoding results yields a global most-likely error (MLE) solution of the original DEM. Our evaluation shows that, with an exact backend, FusionQ matches the monolithic MLE result on every shot. Across decoder backends, FusionQ substantially reduces decoding latency by overlapping local decoding with hardware syndrome acquisition.

AI.tldr: FusionQ is a fusion decoding framework for quantum error correction that derives local decoding tasks from the observed syndrome and fuses them into a single global correction, achieving monolithic MLE-equivalent accuracy while overlapping local decoding with syndrome acquisition to cut latency.
AI.motivation: Conventional QEC decoders rely on fixed decoding instances (a monolithic space-time DEM or a predetermined temporal window) and must wait for enough syndrome data before decoding, forcing every shot through the same global or windowed problem and incurring latency.
AI.method: FusionQ builds open-boundary local DEMs around clusters of fired detectors, expands a cluster's footprint only when a local optimum uses virtual boundary errors, and fuses published local results into one global correction. Backend-agnostic: the scheduler only needs a local solution plus a boundary-use flag, so exact solvers, matching-style decoders on graphlike DEMs, and heuristic decoders share one runtime. A compositional optimality theorem is proved for exact minimum-weight local backends with boundary-free publication.
AI.result: With an exact backend, FusionQ matches the monolithic MLE result on every shot; across decoder backends it substantially reduces decoding latency by overlapping local decoding with hardware syndrome acquisition.
AI.conclusion: Shifting from fixed global/windowed decoding instances to syndrome-driven local tasks with provable compositional optimality preserves accuracy while enabling parallelism and backend flexibility for low-latency QEC decoding.

title: Rational quantum spectral filtering by repeat-until-success protocol
summary: We introduce a finite-memory repeat-until-success (RUS) framework for implementing rational spectral filters on a quantum computer, extending spectral filtering beyond the polynomial transformations implemented by quantum signal processing (QSP) and quantum singular value transformation (QSVT). Our approach interleaves queries to a block encoding of a Hermitian operator $X$, whose spectrum lies in $[-1,1]$, and mid-circuit measurements that either accept, reject, or continue the computation without resetting the quantum state. Although the protocol may run for arbitrarily many rounds, its terminal statistics are determined by a finite-dimensional Lyapunov equation. Under uniform termination and phase-inversion symmetry, we characterize exactly the spectral filters $R(X)$ realizable upon acceptance: $R$ can be any real rational function with no poles on $[-1,1]$ and values in $[0,1]$. We provide a constructive compiler for any admissible $R$, with bounds on memory and expected query cost, and characterize the accepted quantum operation through a spectral coherence kernel. Applications to regularized resolvents and Lorentzian spectroscopy yield exact low-degree realizations and query-cost advantages over the fixed-depth QSVT polynomial-postselection baseline considered here, with all repetitions and independent restarts after rejection included in the cost.

AI.tldr: A finite-memory repeat-until-success (RUS) framework implements arbitrary real rational spectral filters R(X) (no poles on [-1,1], values in [0,1]) on a quantum computer, extending QSP/QSVT polynomial filtering to rational functions via interleaved block-encoding queries and mid-circuit accept/reject/continue measurements.
AI.motivation: QSP and QSVT only realize polynomial (and, with postselection, some non-polynomial) spectral transformations of a Hermitian operator. The authors want to go beyond polynomial transformations to general rational spectral filters, which are useful for tasks like regularized resolvents and Lorentzian spectroscopy, while keeping memory finite and accounting for full query cost.
AI.method: Interleave queries to a block encoding of a Hermitian operator X with spectrum in [-1,1] with mid-circuit measurements that accept, reject, or continue the computation without resetting the state. The protocol can run arbitrarily many rounds but its terminal statistics are governed by a finite-dimensional Lyapunov equation. Under uniform termination and phase-inversion symmetry, the authors characterize the achievable accepted filters R(X) and give a constructive compiler for any admissible real rational R, with bounds on memory and expected query cost, plus a spectral coherence kernel description of the accepted quantum operation.
AI.result: Exact characterization: the realizable accepted filters are exactly real rational functions with no poles on [-1,1] and values in [0,1]. A constructive compiler is provided with memory and expected query-cost bounds. Applications to regularized resolvents and Lorentzian spectroscopy yield exact low-degree realizations and query-cost advantages over the fixed-depth QSVT polynomial-postselection baseline, counting all repetitions and independent restarts after rejection in the cost.
AI.conclusion: Finite-memory RUS provides a provably complete route to rational spectral filtering on quantum computers, strictly generalizing QSP/QSVT polynomial transformations, with efficient constructive compilation and demonstrated cost benefits for resolvent and spectroscopy tasks.

title: Long-range correlated quantum errors from diffuson-correlated dephasing
summary: Electrical solid-state qubits are generally initialized, manipulated and read out through diffusive conductors. We show that the disorder-induced low energy modes of such a conductor --- diffusons --- impose spatially correlated dephasing on any qubits that share it, a mechanism we term diffuson-correlated dephasing. Starting from a Keldysh nonlinear sigma model for the disordered conductive region, coupled capacitively to two-level systems, we obtain the noise kernel in closed form. It decays as the inverse square of the qubit separation and changes sign with the orientation of the pair, so that qubit pairs at equal separation may be correlated or anticorrelated, an unambiguous experimental signature. In two dimensions, the correlated noise a single qubit shares with the rest of the array, in the worst-case scenario, grows logarithmically with array size rather than converging. The sufficient condition for fault tolerance under correlated noise is therefore violated, so standard threshold theorems no longer guarantee protection against this channel for large qubit arrays. As this dephasing originates from the soft-mode content of the environment rather than on any specific gate detail, we expect correlated dephasing channels of this kind wherever solid-state qubits or sensors share a gapless conductive medium.

AI.tldr: Disorder-induced diffuson modes in a shared diffusive conductor impose spatially correlated dephasing on qubits, decaying as inverse-square in separation with orientation-dependent sign, and growing logarithmically with array size in 2D, violating the sufficient condition for fault tolerance under correlated noise.
AI.motivation: Solid-state qubits are initialized, manipulated, and read out via diffusive conductors, yet the correlated dephasing such a shared environment imposes on multiple qubits had not been characterized. The authors aim to identify whether the soft low-energy modes of the disordered conductor generate spatially correlated noise, and whether standard fault-tolerance thresholds still protect large qubit arrays against it.
AI.method: Starting from a Keldysh nonlinear sigma model for the disordered conductive region coupled capacitively to two-level systems, the authors derive the noise kernel in closed form and analyze its spatial structure and scaling with qubit separation and array size.
AI.result: The noise kernel decays as the inverse square of qubit separation and changes sign with pair orientation, so equidistant qubit pairs can be correlated or anticorrelated—an unambiguous experimental signature. In two dimensions, the correlated noise a single qubit shares with the rest of the array grows logarithmically with array size in the worst case rather than converging.
AI.conclusion: Logarithmic growth violates the sufficient condition for fault tolerance under correlated noise, so standard threshold theorems no longer guarantee protection against this channel for large arrays. Because the effect stems from the soft-mode content of the environment rather than gate specifics, diffuson-correlated dephasing is expected wherever solid-state qubits or sensors share a gapless conductive medium.

title: How wide must an eavesdropper be? Leakage of a toric-code logical bit to a strip and the Nishimori point
comment: 19 pages, 4 figures, 11 tables. Code, data, IBM Quantum shot records, transpiled circuits and calibration snapshots in ancillary files. Prepared with AI assistance; see "Use of AI tools"
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computers hand pieces of each logical qubit to separate decoder modules and shared readout lines. How much does a piece reveal? We prove that for any region and any Pauli noise, including correlated noise, an observer's optimal advantage in learning a logical bit is exactly 1 - 2 P_fail, where P_fail is the failure probability of maximum-likelihood decoding confined to that region. Two lessons follow. Geometry, not noise, provides the protection: a region that misses a single column of the code learns exactly nothing at any noise level, while a region that spans the code is protected by noise only at impractical distances (d > 350 for one row at a 10^-3 flip rate). And width is a poor guide to risk: under i.i.d. noise a two-row strip learns exactly as little as one row, yet below threshold an eavesdropper needs a width growing only as ln d. Through the identity, the strip's operational threshold is the Nishimori point of the random-bond Ising model, and a Walsh-Hadamard transfer matrix up to width 16 locates it to within a few thousandths. On two IBM Heron processors (d = 3, 5), an emulated strip adversary shows the predicted jump at width three, and non-uniform qubit errors let a trained attacker profit from the second row that uniform noise makes useless. We turn these results into design rules for partitioned decoding and multiplexed readout. Code and data are included.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that an observer's optimal advantage in learning a logical bit from any region of a fault-tolerant quantum code equals 1 − 2·P_fail, where P_fail is the maximum-likelihood decoding failure probability confined to that region — showing geometry (not noise) provides protection and width is a poor risk guide.
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant architectures split each logical qubit across separate decoder modules and shared readout lines, so each piece may leak partial information. The authors want to quantify exactly how much a region of the code reveals about a logical bit under arbitrary (including correlated) Pauli noise, and to derive design rules for partitioned decoding and multiplexed readout.
AI.method: They prove an identity linking the optimal adversary's advantage to the region-confined maximum-likelihood decoding failure probability. They analyze geometric dependence (columns vs. rows, strip widths), map the strip's operational threshold to the Nishimori point of the random-bond Ising model, and locate it via a Walsh-Hadamard transfer matrix up to width 16. They validate predictions on two IBM Heron processors (d = 3, 5) with an emulated strip adversary, including non-uniform qubit errors.
AI.result: Geometry dominates: a region missing a single code column learns exactly nothing at any noise level, while a full-span row is protected only at impractical distances (d > 350 at 10^-3 flip rate). Width is a poor guide: under i.i.d. noise a two-row strip learns as little as one row, but below threshold an eavesdropper's required width grows only as ln d. The transfer-matrix computation locates the Nishimori point to within a few thousandths. Hardware experiments show the predicted jump at width three, and non-uniform errors let a trained attacker exploit the second row that uniform noise renders useless.
AI.conclusion: The advantage identity yields concrete design rules for partitioned decoding and multiplexed readout: protection stems from code geometry rather than noise level, and width-based risk heuristics are misleading. Practical attackers gain from inhomogeneous error structure, motivating geometry-aware partitioning.

title: Quantized memory of measurement records near the light cone of quantum circuits
summary: Quantum processors now measure qubits in the middle of a circuit, and the stream of outcomes is the raw output of error correction, measurement-based state preparation and monitored dynamics. For a scrambling circuit, predicting the statistics of this stream is as hard as simulating the processor, so there is no exact reference to check it against once the device outgrows classical simulation. We show that near the light cone the problem becomes exactly solvable, for any two-qubit gate. In a brickwork circuit with one polarized qubit in a maximally mixed background, measurements along the edge of the light cone form a two-state Markov chain, and measurements $d$ sites inside the edge are generated by $\lfloor d/2\rfloor+1$ qubits that move with it, while the rest of the chain, however large, acts on them as a memoryless bath. The memory of the record is therefore quantized, one bit on the edge and at most one more for every site of displacement, a bound that generic gates attain. The same causal structure determines which hardware noise the record can see, removes that sensitivity at no gate cost, and yields a tomography-free witness of dual-unitarity. On a 156-qubit superconducting processor, a demonstration with its analysis specified in advance finds the predicted memory one and two sites inside the light cone, and none where the theory forbids it. This gives dynamic circuits an exact reference at any system size, and shows that the collision models of open-system theory arise exactly inside chaotic dynamics.

AI.tldr: Near the edge of a scrambling circuit's light cone, the stream of mid-circuit measurement outcomes is exactly solvable: along the edge it forms a two-state Markov chain, and measurements d sites inside are generated by floor(d/2)+1 co-moving qubits bathed memorylessly by the rest of the chain. This quantizes the record's memory (one bit on the edge, +1 per site of displacement) and was confirmed on a 156-qubit superconducting processor.
AI.motivation: Mid-circuit measurement records (error correction, measurement-based state preparation, monitored dynamics) are hard to predict for scrambling circuits—as hard as simulating the processor—so once the device outgrows classical simulation there is no exact reference to validate the outcome statistics. A scalable, exact benchmark is needed.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of the light-cone edge in brickwork circuits with one polarized qubit in a maximally mixed background, for arbitrary two-qubit gates, establishing exact solvability of outcome statistics: a two-state Markov chain on the edge and effective dynamics of floor(d/2)+1 co-moving qubits with the remainder acting as a memoryless bath. This is tested via a pre-registered demonstration on a 156-qubit superconducting processor.
AI.result: The record's memory is quantized—one bit at the light-cone edge and at most one additional bit per site of displacement—a bound attained by generic gates. The causal structure also identifies which hardware noise the record is sensitive to, allows removing that sensitivity at no gate cost, and provides a tomography-free witness of dual-unitarity. The 156-qubit experiment, with analysis specified in advance, found the predicted memory one and two sites inside the edge, and none where the theory forbids it.
AI.conclusion: Near the light cone, chaotic scrambling dynamics admit an exact, system-size-independent reference for dynamic-circuit output statistics, yielding a lightweight validation protocol for quantum processors. The result also shows that collision models from open-system theory emerge exactly inside chaotic many-body dynamics.

title: Exceptional points in non-Markovian quantum-state diffusion: From coefficient dynamics to state signatures
summary: An exceptional point of a memory-coefficient equation need not have the same signature in every quantum-state observable. We examine this relation within exact non-Markovian quantum-state diffusion (NMQSD), following the same operator closure from its coefficient dynamics to the non-Markovian master equation obtained by noise averaging. A finite homogeneous lift identifies the Jordan chains reached by the causal initialization, while state reconstruction determines which contributions survive in a specified readout. Two models expose the distinction. For common-bath qubits restricted to zero and one excitation, a noise-independent lowering-form $O$ operator gives a closed master equation. Every defective decaying mode transfers its full pole order to a suitable unconditional excitation--reference coherence. A known third-order configuration illustrates both a quadratic--exponential coherence and cancellation of its highest-order term in another quadrature. For a position-coupled oscillator in a fixed-photon-number optomechanical sector, the exact closure contains a scalar noise-history term. On the regular normalizable branch studied for bath decay rates below the oscillator frequency, two second-order coefficient blocks lead to a double pole in the conditional displacement response to the NMQSD noise history, at long preparation age and fixed lag. The purely algebraic coefficient tail cancels from the conditional Gaussian width. Complete noise averaging changes the master-equation coefficients and combines conditional width with the weighted spread of state centers. Together, the models show how causal preparation, state reconstruction, and averaging give coefficient exceptional points a precise, readout-dependent meaning.

AI.tldr: An exceptional point (EP) of the memory-coefficient dynamics is shown to be readout-dependent: its pole order transfers to a quantum-state observable only when causal preparation and state reconstruction let the defective mode survive, and complete noise averaging further reshapes the effect in the non-Markovian master equation.
AI.motivation: Exceptional points are usually attributed to a system's coefficient or generator dynamics, but the same EP need not appear with the same signature in every quantum-state observable. The paper aims to clarify precisely when and how a coefficient-level EP becomes visible in a specified readout within exact non-Markovian quantum-state diffusion (NMQSD).
AI.method: The authors follow a single operator closure from coefficient dynamics through to the non-Markovian master equation obtained by noise averaging. A finite homogeneous lift is used to identify the Jordan chains reached by the causal initialization, and state reconstruction is used to determine which contributions survive in a given readout. Two models are analyzed: (1) common-bath qubits restricted to the zero- and one-excitation subspace with a noise-independent lowering-form O operator giving a closed master equation; (2) a position-coupled oscillator in a fixed-photon-number optomechanical sector, whose exact closure contains a scalar noise-history term, studied on the regular normalizable branch for bath decay rates below the oscillator frequency.
AI.result: For the qubit model, every defective decaying mode transfers its full pole order to a suitable unconditional excitation-reference coherence; a known third-order configuration shows both a quadratic-exponential coherence and cancellation of its highest-order term in another quadrature. For the optomechanical model, two second-order coefficient blocks produce a double pole in the conditional displacement response to the NMQSD noise history at long preparation age and fixed lag, while the purely algebraic coefficient tail cancels from the conditional Gaussian width. Complete noise averaging alters the master-equation coefficients and combines the conditional width with the weighted spread of state centers.
AI.conclusion: Coefficient exceptional points acquire a precise, readout-dependent meaning through three ingredients: causal preparation, state reconstruction, and noise averaging. The same EP can transfer its full pole order to one observable yet be partially or fully cancelled in another, so EP signatures must be assessed per readout rather than inferred from the coefficient equation alone.

title: A Compiler for Fault Tolerant Quantum Computing
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) needs compiler intermediate representations (IRs) that preserve error-correcting-code choices, syndrome information, and non-Clifford resource requirements through analysis, simulation, and hardware lowering. We report practical experience building FTQC, an open-source Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) dialect that makes logical qubits, syndromes, magic states, and Pauli frames typed static single assignment (SSA) values. Its error-correction-aware type system, two-level lowering design, and IR-resident resource analysis provide one inspectable pipeline to Open Quantum Assembly Language~3 (OpenQASM~3), the Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR), Stim, and IQM hardware. Case studies across three code families show that typed metadata makes code-specific decisions verifiable and retargetable: on the 20-qubit Pathfinder at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, decoding reduced logical readout error by 3.3 times. They also expose hidden architectural costs: for a three-qubit Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT-3), a magic-state factory requires five times the peak qubits of the encoded circuit. These experiences demonstrate a practical foundation for developing and evaluating fault-tolerant compiler transformations across software and hardware targets.

AI.tldr: We present FTQC, an open-source MLIR dialect that types logical qubits, syndromes, magic states, and Pauli frames as static SSA values, enabling an error-correction-aware pipeline that lowers to OpenQASM 3, QIR, Stim, and IQM hardware with IR-resident resource analysis.
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing compilers need intermediate representations that preserve error-correcting-code choices, syndrome information, and non-Clifford resource requirements across analysis, simulation, and hardware lowering—capabilities absent from existing IRs.
AI.method: An MLIR dialect making logical qubits, syndromes, magic states, and Pauli frames typed SSA values; contributions include an error-correction-aware type system, a two-level lowering design, and IR-resident resource analysis, yielding one inspectable pipeline to OpenQASM 3, QIR, Stim, and IQM hardware. Case studies span three code families.
AI.result: Typed metadata makes code-specific decisions verifiable and retargetable: on the 20-qubit Pathfinder at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, decoding reduced logical readout error by 3.3x. Hidden architectural costs are exposed—for QFT-3, a magic-state factory requires 5x the peak qubits of the encoded circuit.
AI.conclusion: These practical experiences establish a foundation for developing and evaluating fault-tolerant compiler transformations across software and hardware targets.

title: Early State Exclusion for $5\times5$ Jacobi Matrices
summary: In this paper, we present a problem that arose from quantum computing, when the quantum state to be transferred completely vanishes before the first occurrence of the perfect state transfer. It was posed as an open problem for 1D quantum chains with $n$ of qubits, where $n>4$ is an odd number. We present the solution for $n=5$. The proofs are accessible to students who studied trigonometry and calculus. As for the set-up the knowledge of eigentheory and inner products from linear algebra is needed.

AI.tldr: The paper solves the open case n=5 of the vanishing-state problem in 1D quantum chains, where the quantum state disappears before the first perfect state transfer occurs.
AI.motivation: A problem from quantum computing arises when the quantum state to be transferred vanishes before the first occurrence of perfect state transfer. This was posed as an open problem for 1D quantum chains with n qubits where n>4 is odd, and the paper addresses the first unresolved instance.
AI.method: The authors present a solution for n=5 using elementary analytic tools: the proofs rely on trigonometry and calculus, with the setup requiring eigentheory and inner products from linear algebra.
AI.result: The open problem is resolved for the case n=5, establishing the solution for the first odd chain length beyond the previously known range.
AI.conclusion: The n=5 case of the vanishing-state problem is settled, and the accessible proof style (trigonometry, calculus, elementary linear algebra) makes the result broadly readable for students.

title: The wave equation and two-electron atomic wavefunctions
summary: Axisymmetric solutions of the classical wave equation in three spatial dimensions are shown to be in one-to-one correspondence to functions which annihilate the two-electron kinetic energy operator expressed in coordinates relative to a fixed nucleus.

AI.tldr: Axisymmetric solutions of the 3D classical wave equation correspond one-to-one to functions annihilated by the two-electron kinetic energy operator written in nucleus-relative coordinates.
AI.motivation: The abstract targets a structural link between the free classical wave equation and the quantum-mechanical two-electron kinetic energy operator, presumably to exploit solution methods or simplified models across the two settings.
AI.method: A coordinate transformation from Cartesian space to coordinates relative to a fixed nucleus combined with an axisymmetry restriction, establishing a bijective correspondence between the respective solution spaces.
AI.result: A one-to-one (bijective) correspondence is established between axisymmetric classical wave solutions and functions in the kernel of the two-electron kinetic energy operator in nucleus-relative coordinates.
AI.conclusion: The two apparently distinct problems share the same solution space under the stated symmetry, yielding a mapping that transfers results between classical wave propagation and two-electron kinetic-energy problems.

title: Computational Power of Clifford and Ising Quantum Computers
summary: We extend the efficient classical simulation of Ising quantum computers from braidings to measurements. We investigate several different definitions of efficient Clifford quantum computation by varying the power of the circuit generator. In case the circuit generator can see the entire input, we give a detailed proof that efficient simulation of classical computation would imply the separation of complexity classes $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{PSPACE}$. If the circuit generator sees only the input length, we prove that Clifford quantum computers decide what we call affine languages.

AI.tldr: The paper extends efficient classical simulation of Ising (Clifford) quantum computers from braidings to measurements, and studies how the power of the circuit generator affects the resulting notion of efficient Clifford quantum computation.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed efficient classical simulation of Ising quantum computers for braidings; the authors aim to extend this to measurements and to clarify how different definitions of efficient Clifford computation (depending on the generator's power) change the complexity-theoretic consequences.
AI.method: They investigate several definitions of efficient Clifford quantum computation by varying the power of the circuit generator. For a generator with full access to the input, they relate efficient simulation to a separation of P and PSPACE; for a generator seeing only the input length, they characterize the decided languages as affine languages.
AI.result: With an all-seeing circuit generator, efficient simulation of classical computation would imply a separation of P and PSPACE; with an input-length-only generator, Clifford quantum computers are shown to decide exactly the affine languages.
AI.conclusion: The notion of efficient Clifford quantum computation is sensitive to the circuit generator's power, yielding either a strong complexity-class separation (full input access) or a clean characterization in terms of affine languages (input-length-only access).

title: Syndrome extraction for quantum LDPC codes in silicon: Distributed entanglement and mobile ancillas
comment: 32 pages, 22 figures, 5 tables. Code available at https://github.com/KNFLWNF/singlet-fabric-qldpc
summary: Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes can reduce the number of data qubits required per logical qubit, but their checks require long-range interactions on a planar device. We develop a singlet fabric for bivariate-bicycle codes on a silicon node network. Spin singlets are generated on shuttling lanes and distributed between nodes, where local operations consume them to measure non-local stabilizers. We construct two syndrome-extraction circuits, based on distributed GHZ states and ancilla teleportation, and evaluate them using hardware-constrained schedules and circuit-level memory simulations. We compare these circuits with CAbLECAR, which transports a mobile ancilla between the data qubits of each check. Teleportation can outperform CAbLECAR on its original layout when transport includes spin flips as well as dephasing. Placing the mobile ancilla on our node lattice, however, shortens the mean scheduled route for the [[144,12,12]] Gross code from 350 to 153 $μ$m and lowers its logical error rate up to 50-fold in the sampled bit-flip regime. Direct transport then achieves a lower logical error rate than either singlet circuit at every sampled Gross-code point. With frequent transport bit flips, the GHZ circuit overtakes direct transport once two-qubit gate and readout errors fall below about $4$-$5\times10^{-4}$, roughly half the value assumed here. Fixing the ancilla's data-visit order reveals a trade-off between shorter routes and the correlated errors produced by ancilla faults. Source heralding improves both singlet circuits, whereas phase purification helps the GHZ circuit only above a noise-dependent crossover and worsens teleportation throughout. These results show that the physical layout and interaction order can be as consequential as the choice of extraction circuit, and that cleaner entangled resources do not necessarily produce a more reliable logical memory.

AI.tldr: Bivariate-bicycle qLDPC codes are implemented on a silicon spin-singlet node network; distributed-GHZ and ancilla-teleportation syndrome-extraction circuits are compared against mobile-ancilla transport (CAbLECAR), showing that layout and data-visit order can matter as much as circuit choice.
AI.motivation: qLDPC codes lower the physical-to-logical qubit overhead, but their stabilizer checks require long-range interactions that are costly or impractical on planar hardware. The paper asks how to realize these non-local checks on a distributed device and whether entangled-resource (singlet) approaches can beat simply shuttling a mobile ancilla.
AI.method: A singlet fabric for bivariate-bicycle codes on a silicon node network: spin singlets are generated on shuttling lanes and distributed between nodes, and consumed by local operations to measure non-local stabilizers. Two syndrome-extraction circuits are constructed—one based on distributed GHZ states, one on ancilla teleportation—and benchmarked with hardware-constrained schedules and circuit-level memory simulations, against CAbLECAR (mobile ancilla transported between the data qubits of each check). Sensitivity to transport spin flips/dephasing, ancilla placement on the node lattice, fixed data-visit order, source heralding, and phase purification is examined.
AI.result: Teleportation can beat CAbLECAR on CAbLECAR's original layout when transport carries spin flips as well as dephasing. Placing the mobile ancilla on the node lattice shortens the mean scheduled route for the [[144,12,12]] Gross code from 350 to 153 μm and lowers logical error rate by up to 50× in the sampled bit-flip regime; direct transport then beats both singlet circuits at every sampled point. With frequent transport bit flips, the GHZ circuit overtakes direct transport once two-qubit gate and readout errors drop below ~4–5×10⁻⁴ (about half the assumed value). Fixing the ancilla's data-visit order exposes a trade-off between shorter routes and correlated errors from ancilla faults. Heralding improves both singlet circuits; phase purification helps GHZ only above a noise-dependent crossover and hurts teleportation throughout.
AI.conclusion: Physical layout and interaction order are as consequential as the extraction-circuit choice, and cleaner entangled resources do not necessarily yield a more reliable logical memory.

title: PriorTilt: Decoding quantum LDPC codes with sparse perturbations of belief propagation priors
comment: The implementation source code is available at https://github.com/ionq-publications/PriorTiltDecoder
summary: Although belief propagation (BP) is a widely adopted decoder for classical low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes, its accuracy is limited in the quantum setting. We introduce \PriorTilt{}, a variant of BP obtained by selectively perturbing a small fraction of its prior log-likelihood ratios using offsets determined by recent posterior and outgoing-message statistics, while preserving the same message-passing rules. We compare \PriorTilt{} with Relay-BP and beam search decoders for circuit-level decoding of three benchmark codes. \PriorTilt{} achieves a lower logical error rate (LER) than both baselines at every tested data point. For the $[[144,12,12]]$ Gross code BB144 at noise rate $p=10^{-3}$, the LER reductions reach $4.3\times$ relative to Relay-BP and $3.1\times$ relative to the beam search decoder. At $p=10^{-3}$, \PriorTilt{} has lower mean decoding times than Relay-BP on all three codes and achieves mean decoding speedups of approximately $2.6\times$--$3.0\times$ over the beam search decoder. For BB144 at $p=10^{-3}$, \PriorTilt{} achieves an LER approximately $610\times$ lower than the standard min-sum BP decoder with the same iteration budget, while perturbing fewer than $0.5\%$ of its priors per round on average.

AI.tldr: PriorTilt is a belief-propagation variant that selectively perturbs a small fraction of prior LLRs using offsets derived from recent posterior and outgoing-message statistics, improving logical error rate and decoding speed for circuit-level quantum LDPC decoding.
AI.motivation: Standard belief propagation, while effective for classical LDPC codes, has limited accuracy in the quantum setting, motivating a BP variant that improves decoding without changing the message-passing rules.
AI.method: PriorTilt perturbs a small fraction of prior log-likelihood ratios using offsets determined by recent posterior and outgoing-message statistics, while preserving the same BP message-passing rules. It is compared against Relay-BP and beam search decoders on three benchmark codes under circuit-level decoding.
AI.result: PriorTilt achieves lower LER than both baselines at every tested data point. For the [[144,12,12]] Gross code BB144 at p=1e-3, LER reductions reach 4.3x vs Relay-BP and 3.1x vs beam search. It also has lower mean decoding times than Relay-BP on all three codes and ~2.6x-3.0x speedups over beam search. For BB144 at p=1e-3, LER is ~610x lower than standard min-sum BP with the same iteration budget, while perturbing fewer than 0.5% of priors per round on average.
AI.conclusion: Selective prior perturbation yields substantial LER and speed gains over Relay-BP, beam search, and min-sum BP, with only a minimal perturbation fraction, indicating PriorTilt is an effective and efficient decoder for quantum LDPC codes.

title: Sample complexity of learning fermionic and bosonic Gaussian states with single-copy and entangled measurements
