summary: With single-copy measurements, every mixed fermionic Gaussian state on $m$ modes, pure modes included, is learned to trace distance $ε$ from $Θ(m^3/ε^2)$ copies, with no logarithmic factor, against the known $Θ(m^2/ε^2)$ for collective measurements. We prove the upper bound, resolving Conjecture 10.1 of arXiv:2609.23189 (lower bound for $ε\le1/3600$), and fill most open entries of the sample-complexity table of fermionic and bosonic Gaussian states, for single-copy, $k$-copy and collective measurements. The single-copy measurement's noise is matched to the metric at every occupation scale. With blocks of $k$ copies, the covariant highest-weight measurement of arXiv:2611.07271, read out through the Weyl-shift estimator, is exactly unbiased for every state; it gives $Θ(\max\{m^3/k,m^2\}/ε^2)$ in Frobenius norm on all states and in trace distance on every class at a fixed distance from the pure boundary. The gain $1/k$ ($k\le m$) away from the pure boundary, against $1/\sqrt k$ on cold number-conserving states, is therefore attained. For bosonic Gaussian states with bounded covariance, any displacement and squeezing, and occupations $n_1\le\dots\le n_m$, $O((m^2+r^3+\sum_{i,j>r}1/(n_i+n_j))/ε^2)$ single-copy measurements suffice, $r$ the largest index with $r\,n_r\le2$; this is the minimax rate on dyadic-interval classes, with no spectral gap or cold-mode count assumed, and holds with no covariance bound for displaced passive states. With no bound on energy or squeezing, non-Gaussian measurements learn centred one-mode states, mixed included, from $O(ε^{-2})$ and centred pure $m$-mode states from $O(m^2/ε^2)$ single copies, free of the $\log\log E$ term of Gaussian measurements, and $m$-mode states from $O(m^3/ε^2)$ copies, entangled only in a first round on blocks of $4m+6$.

AI.tldr: This work establishes tight single-copy sample complexities for learning fermionic and bosonic Gaussian states, proving a Θ(m³/ε²) upper bound for mixed fermionic states that resolves a prior conjecture, and filling most entries of the sample-complexity table across single-copy, k-copy, and collective measurement settings.
AI.motivation: Known sample complexities for learning Gaussian states differ by measurement setting and are not fully characterized; a conjecture on the single-copy complexity of mixed fermionic Gaussian states (including pure modes as special cases) remained open, and the sample-complexity table for fermionic and bosonic Gaussian states had unaddressed entries.
AI.method: Single-copy measurements are designed so their noise is matched to the trace-distance metric at every occupation scale. For k-copy blocks, the covariant highest-weight measurement is combined with a Weyl-shift estimator shown to be exactly unbiased. For bosonic states, single-copy protocols exploiting occupation structure (with index r defined by r·n_r ≤ 2) are used. Non-Gaussian measurements are also considered without energy or squeezing bounds.
AI.result: Every mixed fermionic Gaussian state on m modes is learned to trace distance ε from Θ(m³/ε²) copies (no logarithmic factor), matching the Θ(m²/ε²) collective-measurement bound. The k-copy protocol yields Θ(max{m³/k, m²}/ε²) in Frobenius norm, with a 1/k gain (k ≤ m) away from the pure boundary versus 1/√k on cold number-conserving states. Bosonic states with bounded covariance require O((m² + r³ + Σ_{i,j>r} 1/(n_i+n_j))/ε²) single-copy measurements, the minimax rate on dyadic-interval classes. Non-Gaussian measurements achieve O(ε⁻²) for centred one-mode states, O(m²/ε²) for centred pure m-mode states, and O(m³/ε²) for general m-mode states.
AI.conclusion: The results resolve Conjecture 10.1 and fill most open sample-complexity entries, showing single-copy learning of mixed fermionic Gaussian states attains Θ(m³/ε²) with metric-matched noise, that k-copy block measurements achieve optimal 1/k scaling away from the pure boundary, and that bosonic and non-Gaussian protocols reach minimax rates without spectral-gap, cold-mode, or energy assumptions.

title: Double-quantum enhanced coherent control and magnetic sensing of spin defects in hexagonal boron nitride
comment: 13 Pages, 9 figures, accepted in Phys. Rev. Applied
summary: The negatively charged boron vacancy ($V_{\mathrm{B}}^{-}$) in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is a promising spin defect for quantum sensing in two-dimensional material systems. Previous hBN experiments have mainly exploited the two spin-triplet ground-state single-quantum transitions separately. Here we implement a double-quantum driving scheme based on simultaneous resonant microwave excitation of both ground-state single-quantum transitions, establishing coherent control of the $Δm_s=2$ manifold in a $V_{\mathrm{B}}^{-}$ ensemble. We compare the resulting double-quantum response with the corresponding single-quantum protocol under identical experimental conditions. The double-quantum protocol enhances the optical readout contrast and yields a 2.6-fold signal-to-noise improvement in AC magnetometry. We further use the double-quantum relaxation channel as a differential probe of electric-field and strain noise, showing that the present data are compatible with correlated-surface or volume-distributed fluctuations, while short-range uncorrelated surface-noise models are disfavored within the assumptions of our analysis. These results establish double-quantum coherent control and frequency-resolved AC magnetometry in hBN spin ensembles, and identify the sample-dependent measurements needed to determine the microscopic origin of the dominant relaxation channels.

AI.tldr: A double-quantum driving scheme using simultaneous resonant microwave excitation of both ground-state single-quantum transitions establishes coherent control of the Δm_s=2 manifold in hBN V_B^- ensembles, improving AC magnetometry SNR 2.6-fold and enabling differential noise spectroscopy.
AI.motivation: Prior hBN experiments exploited the two spin-triplet ground-state single-quantum transitions of the V_B^- defect separately, leaving the Δm_s=2 double-quantum manifold and its potential sensing advantages unexplored.
AI.method: Simultaneous resonant microwave driving of both ground-state single-quantum transitions in a V_B^- ensemble, compared against a single-quantum protocol under identical experimental conditions; the double-quantum relaxation channel is used as a differential probe of electric-field and strain noise.
AI.result: The double-quantum protocol enhances optical readout contrast and yields a 2.6-fold SNR improvement in AC magnetometry. The data are compatible with correlated-surface or volume-distributed fluctuations, while short-range uncorrelated surface-noise models are disfavored within the analysis assumptions.
AI.conclusion: Double-quantum coherent control and frequency-resolved AC magnetometry are established in hBN spin ensembles, and the sample-dependent measurements needed to identify the microscopic origin of the dominant relaxation channels are identified.

title: Real-time spectral combs from delayed quantum feedback in multimode cavity QED
summary: We study the time-dependent physical spectrum of light for a two-level atom coupled to a large, but discrete, number of modes of an electromagnetic cavity. Radiation emitted by the atom, placed at the center of the cavity, returns after the round-trip time $t_r$, re-excites it, and is re-emitted, producing a sequence of atomic population revivals. For a coupling approximately flat over the atomic linewidth, the emission dynamics reduces to a delay-differential equation of Bixon--Jortner type. Using its analytical solution in terms of Laguerre polynomials, we investigate how successive emission and reabsorption cycles shape the time-dependent spectrum. The physical spectrum exhibits revivals during which a transient frequency comb of spacing $2π/t_r$ develops. The comb results from the quantum interference between successive emission stages; its teeth sit not at the cavity modes but at the resonances of the effective two half-cavities created by the resonantly reflecting atom. The visibility scales as $e^{-Γt_r}$ with the filter bandwidth $Γ$, and at long times the comb converges to the dressed-mode spectrum, which we also obtain analytically in quantitative agreement with exact diagonalization. We show that the physical spectrum resolves the feedback phase, to which the atomic population is insensitive in the regime of well-separated emission stages, and provides additional frequency-resolved signatures of the atomic position. We discuss two feasible experimental implementations of our results with transmons (artificial atoms) coupled to microwave and surface-acoustic-wave resonators.

AI.tldr: Time-dependent spectrum of a two-level atom in a discrete cavity shows periodic population revivals; each revival produces a transient frequency comb spaced by 2π/t_r whose teeth sit at half-cavity resonances, with visibility scaling e^{-Γt_r}.
AI.motivation: Prior treatments of atom-cavity emission focus on population dynamics or steady-state spectra; how successive emission-reabsorption cycles (feedback at round-trip time t_r) shape the frequency-resolved, time-dependent physical spectrum is unclear. The authors aim to resolve the spectrum with a finite-bandwidth filter and identify signatures (feedback phase, atomic position) invisible to population.
AI.method: Model a two-level atom at the center of a discrete multi-mode cavity; for coupling flat over the atomic linewidth, reduce emission dynamics to a Bixon–Jortner-type delay-differential equation and solve analytically via Laguerre polynomials. Compute the time-dependent physical spectrum with a filter of bandwidth Γ, compare to exact diagonalization for the dressed-mode limit, and propose transmon implementations (microwave and SAW resonators).
AI.result: Emission shows a sequence of atomic population revivals; the physical spectrum exhibits revivals containing a transient frequency comb of spacing 2π/t_r arising from interference between successive emission stages. Comb teeth sit at resonances of the effective two half-cavities formed by the resonantly reflecting atom, not at cavity modes. Visibility scales as e^{-Γt_r} and converges at long times to the dressed-mode spectrum, obtained analytically in quantitative agreement with exact diagonalization. The spectrum resolves the feedback phase (invisible to population for well-separated stages) and gives frequency-resolved signatures of atomic position.
AI.conclusion: Feedback-induced revivals imprint a transient, filter-visible frequency comb on the emission spectrum, governed by half-cavity resonances and decaying with Γ; the physical spectrum carries phase and position information beyond population dynamics, and is experimentally accessible with transmon atoms in microwave and SAW resonators.

title: Packet-wise multi-hop quantum routing of hybrid quantum-classical packets
summary: The ability to dynamically route quantum information across multiple nodes is a key requirement for realizing versatile and scalable quantum networks. Quantum routers are devices to achieve packet-level routing beyond static point-to-point connections by handling hybrid packets combining classical headers and quantum payloads. Previously proposed methods have selectively accessed the classical and quantum components of the packets utilizing wavelength splitters and optical switches, and repacked the hybrid packets before transmission through the outgoing link with regenerating classical headers. This work reports a novel optical-fiber-based quantum router that minimizes the disturbance and latency on the hybrid packets through more transparent operation. We experimentally demonstrate double-hop routing via two cascaded routers to three distinct receivers without regeneration of the headers. As a practical application, quantum key distribution packets based on time-bin qubits and a BB84 protocol with a two-decoy-state method are successfully delivered to the three receivers achieving nonzero secret key rates. These results demonstrate the feasibility of extensive quantum networks interconnected by multiple-step router nodes.

AI.tldr: The paper experimentally demonstrates a fiber-based quantum router that routes hybrid packets (classical headers + quantum payloads) transparently, achieving double-hop routing through two cascaded routers to three receivers without header regeneration and delivering QKD (time-bin BB84 with two-decoy states) with nonzero secret key rates.
AI.motivation: Scalable, versatile quantum networks require packet-level routing across multiple nodes beyond static point-to-point links. Prior routers rely on wavelength splitters and optical switches to separately access classical/quantum components and regenerate headers before retransmission, introducing disturbance and latency on hybrid packets. The work aims to minimize this disturbance and latency.
AI.method: A novel optical-fiber-based quantum router is proposed and built to operate more transparently on hybrid packets. Double-hop routing is experimentally demonstrated via two cascaded routers delivering packets to three distinct receivers without regenerating the classical headers. Practical validation uses QKD packets based on time-bin qubits with a BB84 protocol and a two-decoy-state method.
AI.result: Double-hop routing through two cascaded routers succeeds to three distinct receivers with no header regeneration. QKD packets are successfully delivered to the three receivers, each achieving nonzero secret key rates.
AI.conclusion: Transparent, low-disturbance fiber-based quantum routing is feasible, supporting multistep router-node interconnection and demonstrating the practicality of extensive, scalable quantum networks.

title: Machine-learning decoders for fusion-based quantum computing in real time
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires decoders that combine accuracy, throughput, low latency, and scalability to large numbers of physical qubits. In photonic fusion-based architectures, erasures from photon loss and probabilistic fusion measurements are a dominant error mechanism, motivating decoders that remain accurate at high erasure rates. We introduce PRISM, a transformer-based machine-learning decoder designed to exploit the known locations of erasures in protocols subject to both Pauli and erasure errors. We benchmark PRISM across a wide range of fault-tolerant protocols based on surface codes, color codes, and quantum low-density parity-check codes, with distances up to 24. Across these benchmarks, PRISM matches the logical error rates of integer-programming-based decoders while being significantly faster, including at error rates up to 50% of threshold. We further optimize the decoder and its real-time hardware implementation to reduce latency while maintaining accuracy. Our optimized implementation on an AMD VP1902 FPGA can decode logical blocks of distance 8 in both space and time, demonstrating a latency of 6.59 microseconds and an amortized decoding time of 1.56 microseconds per logical block is possible. These results show that machine-learning decoding can provide accurate, low-latency inference for erasure-dominated fault-tolerant quantum architectures.

AI.tldr: PRISM is a transformer-based machine-learning decoder that exploits known erasure locations in photonic fusion-based fault-tolerant quantum architectures, matching integer-programming decoder accuracy while being much faster, with an FPGA implementation achieving microsecond-scale latency.
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computation needs decoders that are simultaneously accurate, high-throughput, low-latency, and scalable to many physical qubits. In photonic fusion-based architectures, photon loss and probabilistic fusion measurements produce erasures that dominate error mechanisms, so decoders must stay accurate at high erasure rates.
AI.method: The authors introduce PRISM, a transformer-based ML decoder that exploits the known locations of erasures in protocols subject to both Pauli and erasure errors. It is benchmarked across surface codes, color codes, and quantum LDPC codes with distances up to 24. The decoder and its real-time hardware implementation are further optimized for latency, with deployment on an AMD VP1902 FPGA.
AI.result: PRISM matches logical error rates of integer-programming-based decoders while being significantly faster, including at error rates up to 50% of threshold. The optimized FPGA implementation decodes distance-8 logical blocks in both space and time with 6.59 microseconds latency and 1.56 microseconds amortized decoding time per logical block.
AI.conclusion: Machine-learning decoding can deliver accurate, low-latency inference for erasure-dominated fault-tolerant quantum architectures, making it a viable practical decoding approach.

title: An Efficient Quantum Algorithm for Preparing Uniform Superpositions over Arbitrary Integer Intervals
summary: We consider exact preparation of the uniform quantum state supported on an arbitrary nonempty interval of integer labels in an $n$-qubit register. For every $0\leq a<a+M\leq2^n$, we give an ancilla-free circuit using only one-qubit gates and singly controlled one-qubit gates. In the logical gate model specified in the paper, the direct construction has exact worst-case gate count $5n-9$ for $n\geq3$; its exact maxima for $n=1$ and $n=2$ are $1$ and $3$, respectively. A worst-case lower bound of $Ω(n)$ establishes asymptotic optimality in the register width. In addition, the gate complexity admits an instance-dependent bound $O(\log_2 M+ε)$, where $ε$ is an offset-dependent parameter defined in terms of binary Hamming weights. We also derive a reflected construction and a classical procedure that selects the lower-count exact circuit. The direct construction admits an $O(n)$ logical-depth upper bound. We also treat bitwise-XOR images of intervals and arithmetic progressions with power-of-two spacing.

AI.tldr: An ancilla-free, exact circuit prepares uniform superpositions over arbitrary integer intervals [a, a+M) in an n-qubit register using only one-qubit and singly controlled one-qubit gates, with worst-case exact gate count 5n−9 (optimal in Θ(n) sense).
AI.motivation: Preparing uniform quantum states on arbitrary contiguous label intervals is a basic primitive (state preparation, amplitude loading, search/QFT-style subroutines), but exact, ancilla-free constructions with tight gate counts and provable lower bounds were lacking.
AI.method: Give a direct ancilla-free construction using one-qubit gates and singly controlled one-qubit gates in a specified logical gate model. Prove an Ω(n) worst-case lower bound, derive an instance-dependent bound O(log2 M + ε) with ε tied to binary Hamming weights, give a reflected (mirror) construction, an O(n) logical-depth bound, and a classical selector procedure choosing the minimum-count exact circuit; extend to bitwise-XOR images of intervals and power-of-two-spaced arithmetic progressions.
AI.result: Worst-case exact gate count 5n−9 for n≥3 (exact maxima 1 and 3 for n=1,2); Ω(n) lower bound gives asymptotic optimality in register width; instance-dependent complexity O(log2 M + ε); O(n) logical depth; selector picks lower-count of direct vs reflected circuits.
AI.conclusion: Exact, ancilla-free interval-uniform state preparation achieves asymptotically optimal Θ(n) gate cost with small constants, low depth, instance-adaptive refinements, and extensions to XOR-transformed intervals and sparse arithmetic progressions.

title: Observation of strong electric dipole-dipole interactions between two atoms
summary: We have prepared pairs of atoms at densities exceeding $ 10^{16}/\rm{cm}^3$ corresponding to $n\lambdabar^3>10$ and studied how they interact with light. In this regime, the coherent part of the electric dipole-dipole interaction is larger than the dissipative part, and a single photon emission can transfer large momenta (larger than ten times the single photon recoil) to the atoms. For off-resonant laser light, the atoms are dressed with an electric dipole moment of $\approx$ 1 Debye and interact coherently. This light-induced dipole-dipole interaction has been previously observed only in the far-field mean-field regime. For two atoms, the resonance is shifted by the two-body Lamb shift which is dominated by the near-field part of the dipolar interaction. Dipolar resonance shifts have been observed before only for many atoms interacting with the far-field part of the dipolar interaction. Our work sheds new light on photoassociation processes and paves the way for studying driven quantum systems with strong electric dipole-dipole interactions.

AI.tldr: The authors prepared atomic pairs at densities exceeding 10^16/cm^3 (nλ̄^3 > 10) and studied their light interaction, observing coherence-dominated dipole-dipole interactions, large momentum transfer per emitted photon, ~1 Debye light-induced dipoles, and a two-body Lamb shift dominated by the near-field dipolar term.
AI.motivation: Prior observations of light-induced and dipolar resonance shifts were limited to the far-field mean-field regime and many-atom systems; the near-field, few-body, high-density regime remained largely unexplored, motivating study of coherent electric dipole-dipole interactions where the coherent part exceeds the dissipative part.
AI.method: Pairs of atoms were prepared at densities above 10^16/cm^3 (nλ̄^3 > 10) and probed with off-resonant laser light, which dresses the atoms with an electric dipole moment of ~1 Debye, enabling coherent dipole-dipole interaction; the two-body resonance shift was measured and attributed to the near-field part of the dipolar interaction.
AI.result: The coherent part of the electric dipole-dipole interaction exceeds the dissipative part; a single photon emission can transfer momenta greater than ten times the single-photon recoil; a two-body Lamb shift dominates the resonance shift and is governed by the near-field dipolar term, in contrast to previously observed far-field-dominated many-body shifts.
AI.conclusion: The work provides new insight into photoassociation processes and opens a path toward studying driven quantum systems with strong electric dipole-dipole interactions in the near-field, few-body, high-density regime.

title: Quantum-Assisted Generative Anomaly Detection: A Dimension-Controlled Study of Latent Refinement
summary: Anomaly-based malware detectors learn what benign files look like and flag deviations. Generative approaches to this problem can make use of a "latent" or "prior" data representation, which is often chosen to be a Gaussian distribution. We ask whether the choice of prior distribution matters, and whether one produced by quantum hardware behaves differently from a classical one. Building on SAGEGAN, a style-based detector trained only on benign data, we compare three latent distributions: the original 512-dimensional Gaussian, a 48-dimensional Gaussian, and a 48-dimensional distribution sampled from an ORCA Computing PT-2 photonic quantum processor. We then refine each trained model's frozen representation using greedy and reinforcement-learning methods. Across ten random seeds, the quantum-derived model shows richer internal structure with better effective rank and latent similarity. It also benefits most from refinement. Though final detection accuracy is similar to that of the refined Gaussian latent, these findings show differences in latent geometry and refinement behavior between the trained configurations.

AI.tldr: The paper compares the effect of latent prior distribution choice in an anomaly-based malware detector, contrasting a classical Gaussian prior with a quantum-hardware-sampled prior, and examines how each interacts with representation refinement.
AI.motivation: Generative anomaly detection relies on a latent/prior representation typically assumed to be Gaussian, but whether the choice of prior matters—and whether a quantum-derived prior behaves differently from a classical one—is unexplored.
AI.method: Building on SAGEGAN (a style-based detector trained only on benign data), the authors train three variants with different latent distributions: the original 512-D Gaussian, a 48-D Gaussian, and a 48-D distribution sampled from an ORCA Computing PT-2 photonic quantum processor. Each trained model's frozen representation is then refined using greedy and reinforcement-learning methods, evaluated across ten random seeds.
AI.result: The quantum-derived model exhibits richer internal structure, with better effective rank and latent similarity, and benefits most from refinement. Final detection accuracy, however, is comparable to that of the refined Gaussian latent.
AI.conclusion: The choice of prior distribution affects latent geometry and refinement behavior even when detection accuracy is similar, indicating that prior selection shapes internal representation structure rather than end-task performance alone.

title: A Hardware-Trained Generative Quantum Eigensolver for Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization of Organotin Hydroxides up to 70 Qubits
comment: 76 pages (26 pages main text, 50 pages appendices), 24 figures, 38 tables
summary: Quantum hardware can provide feedback for training circuit generators beyond the reach of exact classical simulation. We train generative quantum eigensolver (GQE) policies, transformers conditioned on molecular descriptors, to generate the state-preparation circuits for sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD). Training runs first on a noiseless simulator and then with the IBM Heron processor ibm_kobe inside the loop, at 46 and 70 qubits ($1.2 \times 10^8$ shots for the four main training runs). A classical CCSD(T) reference energy of the training molecules enters only an admission gate and two auxiliary reward terms. During hardware training, a reward penalty prevents collapse to circuits that sample only the Hartree-Fock determinant. Policies trained on transition-metal complexes are applied without retraining to Sn(OH)$_3$-Me and its hydrates, minimal models of organotin photoresists for extreme-ultraviolet lithography, from 32 to 70 qubits. After one round of hardware sampling, followed by classical ranking and recovery of the cached counts with the molecular Hamiltonian and no further QPU calls, 27 of 28 runs at 46-70 qubits are within 15 mHa of the density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) reference (median 4.5 mHa), and in all eight runs with an untrained control the trained policy is more accurate. At 56-70 qubits the selected circuits use 34-72 times fewer two-qubit gates than the local unitary cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) circuit transpiled for the same device. These results demonstrate that circuit generators can be trained with quantum hardware at 70 qubits.

AI.tldr: Generative quantum eigensolver (GQE) policies are trained with an IBM 70-qubit processor in the loop to produce state-preparation circuits for sample-based quantum diagonalization, yielding near-DMRG accuracy with drastically fewer two-qubit gates.
AI.motivation: Training circuit generators for quantum chemistry is limited by exact classical simulation, so a method that uses quantum hardware itself as the training feedback signal is needed to scale circuit generation toward chemically relevant system sizes.
AI.method: Transformer-based GQE policies conditioned on molecular descriptors are trained first on a noiseless simulator and then with the IBM Heron processor ibm_kobe in the loop at 46 and 70 qubits (1.2e8 shots across four main runs). CCSD(T) enters only an admission gate and two auxiliary reward terms; a reward penalty prevents collapse to Hartree-Fock-only sampling. Policies trained on transition-metal complexes are transferred without retraining to Sn(OH)3-Me and its hydrates (32-70 qubits). Classical ranking and cached-count recovery with the molecular Hamiltonian follow a single hardware sampling round with no further QPU calls.
AI.result: 27 of 28 runs at 46-70 qubits lie within 15 mHa of the DMRG reference (median 4.5 mHa); in all eight untrained-control comparisons the trained policy is more accurate. At 56-70 qubits the selected circuits use 34-72x fewer two-qubit gates than the transpiled LUCJ circuit for the same device.
AI.conclusion: Circuit generators can be trained with quantum hardware in the loop at up to 70 qubits, enabling accurate, gate-efficient state-preparation circuits for quantum diagonalization and transferable application to chemically relevant models.

title: Polynomial Quantum Recurrent Channels for Matrix Inverse Actions: Deferred-Reset Dynamics and Chebyshev Filtering
summary: We develop completely positive, trace-preserving polynomial recurrent channels for quantum solution-state preparation and derive fixed-point and time-varying tracking bounds. Across 2,880 synthetic configurations, resident Chebyshev recurrence improves accuracy-passing snapshot counts in 608 cases, ties in 2,271, and loses in one. A separate 360-scenario cost study shows that fresh recurrence is cheaper in all 184 jointly feasible scenarios (median resident-to-fresh cost ratio: 3.12), while resident recurrence uniquely satisfies accuracy requirements in 74 cases. At a logical noise rate of $10^-4$, neither recurrent method qualifies. Based on exact reduced-density simulations and assumed cost models, our results demonstrate conditional tracking advantages but no general end-to-end speedup or total-cost benefit.

AI.tldr: Completely positive trace-preserving polynomial recurrent channels are developed for quantum solution-state preparation; across 2,880 synthetic configurations resident Chebyshev recurrence improves accuracy-passing snapshots in 608 cases, ties in 2,271, loses in one, and fresh recurrence is cheaper in all 184 jointly feasible scenarios (median cost ratio 3.12), but neither recurrent method qualifies at logical noise 1e-4, so advantages are conditional with no general end-to-end speedup.
AI.motivation: The paper seeks to determine whether recurrent (resident vs. fresh) polynomial channel schemes for quantum solution-state preparation yield practical accuracy and cost benefits, and under what conditions such advantages hold rather than assuming a general speedup.
AI.method: Completely positive, trace-preserving polynomial recurrent channels are constructed, with derived fixed-point and time-varying tracking bounds; evaluation uses exact reduced-density simulations with assumed cost models across 2,880 synthetic configurations plus a separate 360-scenario cost study comparing resident and fresh Chebyshev recurrence.
AI.result: Resident Chebyshev recurrence improves accuracy-passing snapshot counts in 608 cases, ties in 2,271, loses in one; fresh recurrence is cheaper in all 184 jointly feasible scenarios (median resident-to-fresh cost ratio 3.12), while resident recurrence uniquely meets accuracy requirements in 74 cases; at logical noise 1e-4 neither recurrent method qualifies.
AI.conclusion: Conditional tracking advantages are demonstrated, but no general end-to-end speedup or total-cost benefit is established; recurrent polynomial channels are competitive only in specific accuracy- or cost-driven regimes.

title: Eigenmode and field imaging of a compact superconducting resonator array
summary: Superconducting resonator arrays can tailor the photonic environment for quantum information processing, but conventional port-based microwave spectroscopy alone does not resolve the rich spatial structure of their modes. Here, we apply laser scanning microscopy (LSM) and nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center magnetometry to a two-dimensional superconducting resonator array consisting of 33 lumped-element resonators arranged in a honeycomb lattice hosting topological edge states. We demonstrate the complementarity of the two techniques: LSM images the eigenmodes, while NV magnetometry maps the local microwave magnetic field amplitude. Using this spatial information, we experimentally validate that the realized lattice matches the design, we image the topological edge state and measure its sublattice polarization, and place an upper bound of $\approx0.3\%$ on the relative on-site frequency disorder in the lattice. Our work establishes a combined spatial characterization approach for compact superconducting resonator arrays with applications in hybrid spin--superconducting quantum systems.

AI.tldr: The authors combine laser scanning microscopy (LSM) and NV-center magnetometry to spatially characterize a honeycomb superconducting lumped-element resonator array hosting topological edge states, imaging eigenmodes, validating lattice design, measuring edge-state sublattice polarization, and bounding on-site frequency disorder.
AI.motivation: Conventional port-based microwave spectroscopy cannot resolve the spatial structure of modes in superconducting resonator arrays, which is needed to verify designed lattices and topological states.
AI.method: A two-dimensional array of 33 lumped-element superconducting resonators in a honeycomb lattice is characterized using LSM to image eigenmodes and NV-center magnetometry to map local microwave magnetic field amplitude, exploiting the complementarity of the two techniques.
AI.result: The realized lattice matches the design; the topological edge state is imaged and its sublattice polarization measured; the relative on-site frequency disorder is bounded to about 0.3%.
AI.conclusion: The combined spatial characterization approach is established for compact superconducting resonator arrays, with relevance to hybrid spin–superconducting quantum systems.

title: Analog quantum approximate optimization algorithm for solving the weighted MaxCut problem on three-dimensional single-atom Rydberg array
summary: We theoretically investigate an analog implementation of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) for the weighted maximum cut problem (MaxCut) problem. The protocol uses a three-dimensional array of individually trapped Rydberg atoms driven by globally addressed laser pulses, with site-dependent detunings applied near the Rydberg resonance. As benchmarks, we consider twenty randomly weighted 3-regular graphs with 12 vertices each. Problem weights are encoded directly in the interatomic interaction energies by choosing appropriate three-dimensional atom positions. We compare two parameter-optimization strategies: discretized quantum annealing and warm-start initialization using a graph neural network (GNN). The combined optimization strategy creates a portfolio that outperforms the Goemans-Williamson (GW) rounding almost in all instances in the noiseless case. We analyze the sampling statistics and the total pulse-time cost of both approaches. Finally, we emulate the performance of the optimized schedules on quantum trajectories using a realistic error model of the Aquila neutral-atom quantum processor.

AI.tldr: The paper theoretically studies an analog QAOA protocol for weighted MaxCut on a 3D array of individually trapped Rydberg atoms with global laser pulses and site-dependent detunings, benchmarked on twenty 12-vertex weighted 3-regular graphs, comparing discretized quantum annealing and GNN warm-start optimization.
AI.motivation: Weighted MaxCut is a hard combinatorial optimization problem, and near-term Rydberg atom arrays offer a natural analog platform where problem weights can be directly encoded in interatomic interaction energies. The authors aim to assess whether analog QAOA on such hardware can beat classical approximation guarantees (GW rounding) and to characterize practical optimization and error trade-offs.
AI.method: Three-dimensional array of individually trapped Rydberg atoms driven by globally addressed laser pulses, with site-dependent detunings applied near the Rydberg resonance. Problem weights are encoded in interaction energies through chosen 3D atom positions. Benchmarks: twenty randomly weighted 3-regular graphs with 12 vertices. Two parameter-optimization strategies compared: discretized quantum annealing and warm-start initialization via a graph neural network (GNN), forming a combined portfolio. Sampling statistics and total pulse-time cost analyzed, and optimized schedules emulated on quantum trajectories with a realistic Aquila error model.
AI.result: The combined optimization portfolio outperforms Goemans-Williamson rounding in almost all instances in the noiseless case. Sampling statistics and pulse-time costs of both optimization approaches are characterized, and performance under a realistic Aquila error model is emulated via quantum trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Analog QAOA with site-dependent detunings on 3D Rydberg atom arrays, combined with hybrid annealing/GNN warm-start optimization, is a promising route to surpass classical GW guarantees on weighted MaxCut, though real-device noise (Aquila) remains a key limiting factor.

title: Coherent Optical Readout of Neutral-Atom Qubits via Homodyne Detection of Resonant Fluorescence
summary: Fast, non-destructive qubit readout is essential for repeated sampling, mid-circuit measurement, and fault-tolerant neutral-atom quantum processing, but camera-based fluorescence detection introduces electronic latency beyond fluorescence-collection time. We propose coherent readout of the state-dependent resonant fluorescence using balanced homodyne detection with photodiodes. An analytic model quantifies the effect of atomic motion on the time-integrated quadrature signal and noise, showing that harmonic motion causes phase averaging while photon recoils produce trajectory-dependent signal fluctuations; the competition between signal accumulation and motion-induced decoherence sets an optimal detection time. Three-dimensional Monte Carlo simulations validate the model and predict state-detection fidelities exceeding 99% within 100 $μ\mathrm{s}$ for experimentally realistic parameters. These results establish the readout conditions and physical constraints for rapid coherent fluorescence readout of neutral-atom qubits.

AI.tldr: We propose coherent readout of state-dependent resonant fluorescence via balanced homodyne detection with photodiodes to overcome camera latency in neutral-atom qubit readout, with a model and 3D Monte Carlo simulations predicting >99% fidelity within 100 μs.
AI.motivation: Fast, non-destructive qubit readout is needed for repeated sampling, mid-circuit measurement, and fault-tolerant neutral-atom quantum processing, but camera-based fluorescence detection adds electronic latency beyond the fluorescence-collection time.
AI.method: Balanced homodyne detection with photodiodes for coherent readout of state-dependent resonant fluorescence; an analytic model quantifies atomic-motion effects on the time-integrated quadrature signal and noise (harmonic motion causes phase averaging, photon recoils cause trajectory-dependent signal fluctuations); 3D Monte Carlo simulations validate the model.
AI.result: The competition between signal accumulation and motion-induced decoherence sets an optimal detection time; simulations predict state-detection fidelities exceeding 99% within 100 μs for experimentally realistic parameters.
AI.conclusion: The results establish the readout conditions and physical constraints for rapid coherent fluorescence readout of neutral-atom qubits.

title: Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM): A Unified Learning-Based Framework for Noise Resilience in Quantum Machine Learning
summary: Error mitigation stands between variational quantum algorithms and useful results on today's noisy hardware, yet in practice a mitigation method is usually chosen once, by hand, and applied unchanged for the life of an experiment. This is a poor fit for quantum machine learning (QML), where the circuit and the noise drift as training proceeds, so the best strategy in one regime is often wrong in another. We present a generalized form of Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM), which treats the choice of mitigation technique as an online decision made from an algorithm's own feedback. A single contextual-bandit controller observes signals any variational algorithm already produces, such as fidelity, entropy, reward or loss, and gradient behavior, and selects among Zero-Noise Extrapolation, Probabilistic Error Cancellation, Measurement Error Mitigation, Dynamical Decoupling, and circuit optimization per step. Because it depends only on this shared feedback interface, the framework applies unchanged across supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, and hybrid quantum-classical learning. Evaluated on five paradigms across 80 algorithm-and-noise conditions, adaptive selection reaches 95.5% of an oracle that always picks the best technique and significantly outperforms all six fixed strategies (Friedman $χ^{2}=92.18$, $p\approx1.1\times10^{-17}$; pairwise Wilcoxon $p<4\times10^{-6}$). The learned policy is noise-aware: its favored technique shifts as depolarizing and readout error rise. On noise models from eight real IBM devices, APGEM tracks the oracle almost exactly (99.9% of oracle utility) at a flat cost of roughly $1.3\times10^{4}$ shots from three to eight qubits.

AI.tldr: APGEM treats the choice of quantum error-mitigation technique as an online contextual-bandit decision driven by a variational algorithm's own feedback, and selects among five techniques per step. It reaches 95.5% of oracle utility across 80 algorithm-and-noise conditions and 99.9% on eight real IBM noise models at ~1.3×10^4 shots.
AI.motivation: In current practice a mitigation method is chosen once by hand and fixed for the whole experiment, which poorly fits QML where circuit structure and noise drift during training, so the optimal strategy in one regime is often suboptimal in another.
AI.method: A generalized Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation framework uses a single contextual-bandit controller that observes signals any variational algorithm already emits (fidelity, entropy, reward/loss, gradient behavior) and selects per step among Zero-Noise Extrapolation, Probabilistic Error Cancellation, Measurement Error Mitigation, Dynamical Decoupling, and circuit optimization. It relies only on a shared feedback interface, so it applies unchanged to supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, and hybrid quantum-classical learning.
AI.result: Across five paradigms and 80 algorithm-and-noise conditions, adaptive selection achieves 95.5% of an always-best oracle and significantly outperforms six fixed strategies (Friedman χ²=92.18, p≈1.1×10⁻¹⁷; pairwise Wilcoxon p<4×10⁻⁶). The learned policy is noise-aware, shifting preferred techniques as depolarizing and readout error increase. On noise models from eight real IBM devices it tracks the oracle at 99.9% of utility with flat cost of roughly 1.3×10⁴ shots from three to eight qubits.
AI.conclusion: Error mitigation is better framed as an online, feedback-driven policy-selection problem than as a static configuration; a single bandit controller generalizes across learning paradigms, adapts to noise regime, and approaches oracle performance at modest fixed shot cost.

title: Correlations carried and controlled by coupled non-Markovian environments
comment: 6 main-text figures; Supplemental Material with 6 additional figures included
summary: An environment can retain quantum information and carry it between spatially separated systems. Describing the combined influence of these processes requires a treatment of both environmental memory and spatial correlations. Here, we formulate a local hierarchy of pure states for quantum systems coupled to spatially correlated, non-Markovian environments whose modes themselves exchange excitations. We use this method to describe the reduced spin dynamics of a chain of locally coupled Rabi spin--cavity pairs motivated by cavity-QED implementations, where photon hopping in the eliminated cavity environment generates correlations and entanglement between otherwise isolated spins. Monitoring intermediate cavities and feeding their measurement records back onto the corresponding spins further enhances correlations between endpoint spins that receive no direct feedback. The delayed response when feedback starts, and continued entanglement growth after it stops, support a mechanism in which coherent environmental dynamics carry the effects of earlier feedback to the endpoint spins. Finally, tensor-network simulations of XXZ and Heisenberg chains show how environmental transport changes many-body correlation patterns. These results show how coupled environments and local feedback can control correlations between distant spins. We provide a numerically exact stochastic pure-state framework for simulating these processes, opening up avenues to explore the coherent and dissipative control of interacting non-Markovian many-body systems.

AI.tldr: The authors develop a local hierarchy of pure states (HOPS) framework to simulate quantum systems coupled to spatially correlated, non-Markovian environments whose modes exchange excitations, and use it to show how photon hopping in a cavity environment, combined with local measurement feedback, generates and controls correlations and entanglement between distant spins.
AI.motivation: Environments can store and transport quantum information between spatially separated systems, but describing this requires simultaneously treating environmental memory (non-Markovianity) and spatial correlations among environmental modes. Existing methods typically handle one but not both, so a numerically exact framework for such coupled, structured environments is needed.
AI.method: They formulate a local hierarchy of pure states for quantum systems coupled to spatially correlated non-Markovian environments whose modes themselves exchange excitations. They apply it to a chain of locally coupled Rabi spin–cavity pairs (cavity-QED motivated), where photon hopping in the eliminated cavity environment mediates correlations between otherwise isolated spins. Intermediate cavities are monitored and their measurement records fed back onto the corresponding spins. Tensor-network simulations of XXZ and Heisenberg chains are also performed.
AI.result: Photon hopping in the eliminated cavity environment generates correlations and entanglement between otherwise isolated spins; monitoring intermediate cavities and feeding back their records enhances correlations between endpoint spins that receive no direct feedback. A delayed response when feedback starts and continued entanglement growth after it stops support a mechanism in which coherent environmental dynamics transport the effects of earlier feedback to the endpoint spins. Tensor-network simulations show environmental transport reshapes many-body correlation patterns in XXZ and Heisenberg chains.
AI.conclusion: Coupled environments and local feedback can control correlations between distant spins. The work provides a numerically exact stochastic pure-state framework for simulating these processes, opening avenues for coherent and dissipative control of interacting non-Markovian many-body systems.

title: Reservoir-induced Quantum Phase Transitions in spin ensembles
summary: In this work, we present a comprehensive analysis of an open quantum system consisting of a collection of N two-level atoms in the thermodynamic limit coupled to bosonic reservoirs. Our results demonstrate that, when the system-bath interactions lacks a metastable minimum, as in the counterterm-free case, the system can undergo a quantum phase transition set by the reservoir structure rather than by coherent internal dynamics. Using exact quantum Langevin equations, valid even in the overdamped regime near criticality, where the loss rates can exceed the resonance frequency of the softening mode, we locate the critical point via the complex excitation spectrum and obtain closed-form reflection and transmission spectra that display the mode softening and an increasingly asymmetric lineshape near the transition.

AI.tldr: A collection of N two-level atoms coupled to bosonic reservoirs in the thermodynamic limit can undergo a bath-induced quantum phase transition when the system-bath interaction has no metastable minimum (e.g., counterterm-free case); the critical point is located via the complex excitation spectrum, and the softening mode with increasingly asymmetric lineshapes is captured in closed-form reflection/transmission spectra.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to characterize open quantum systems of many two-level atoms coupled to bosonic baths, specifically to determine what drives criticality when coherent internal dynamics are absent—i.e., whether the reservoir structure itself can set a quantum phase transition, including in the overdamped regime where loss rates exceed the softening-mode frequency.
AI.method: Exact quantum Langevin equations valid beyond the weak-damping/underdamped approximation (applicable near criticality where loss rates can exceed the resonance frequency); analysis of the complex excitation spectrum to locate the critical point; closed-form derivation of reflection and transmission spectra from the reservoir-coupled dynamics.
AI.result: When the system-bath interaction lacks a metastable minimum (counterterm-free case), the system undergoes a quantum phase transition governed by the reservoir spectral structure rather than by coherent internal dynamics. The transition is identified through the complex excitation spectrum, and the reflection/transmission spectra show mode softening plus an increasingly asymmetric lineshape approaching the critical point.
AI.conclusion: Reservoir structure alone can drive a quantum phase transition in thermodynamic-limit atomic ensembles, and exact Langevin treatment extends valid predictions to the overdamped critical regime, providing experimentally relevant spectral signatures (softening and asymmetric lineshapes) for detecting the transition.

title: Multiparameter quantum estimation of circulant networks
summary: Networks provide a natural description of interaction patterns, transport media, and communication architectures. Accurately characterizing their coupling structure is a key challenge in quantum technologies. We investigate the multiparameter quantum estimation of coupling strengths in circulant networks probed by continuous-time quantum walks. We derive the quantum Fisher information matrix, identify the optimal probe states and determine the ultimate precision allowed by quantum measurements, together with its scaling with the number of unknown couplings. We further analyze the precision achievable through position measurements of the walker, comparing the corresponding classical Cramér-Rao bounds for optimal and localized probe states with the quantum limit. Finally, we consider finite-resolution detection modeled by coarse-grained position measurements. Although coarse graining generally reduces estimation precision, we find that lower-resolution measurements can, in some instances, outperform other measurements with finer spatial resolution. Our results provide a systematic characterization of the fundamental and practical limits of coupling estimation in quantum-walk-based network inference.

AI.tldr: The paper characterizes fundamental and practical limits of estimating coupling strengths in circulant networks probed by continuous-time quantum walks, deriving the quantum Fisher information matrix, optimal probe states, quantum scaling limits, and comparing them with classical Cramér-Rao bounds under position and coarse-grained measurements.
AI.motivation: Networks naturally describe interaction patterns and communication architectures, and accurately characterizing their coupling structure is a key challenge in quantum technologies. A systematic understanding of the ultimate and practically achievable precision for coupling estimation in quantum-walk-based network inference is lacking.
AI.method: The authors investigate multiparameter quantum estimation of coupling strengths in circulant networks probed by continuous-time quantum walks. They derive the quantum Fisher information matrix, identify optimal probe states, determine the quantum limit and its scaling with the number of unknown couplings, and analyze position measurements via classical Cramér-Rao bounds for optimal and localized probe states. They also model finite-resolution detection through coarse-grained position measurements.
AI.result: The quantum Fisher information matrix and optimal probe states are obtained, yielding the ultimate precision and its scaling with the number of unknown couplings. Classical Cramér-Rao bounds for optimal and localized probe states are compared with the quantum limit. Coarse graining generally reduces precision, but lower-resolution measurements can in some instances outperform finer-resolution ones.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a systematic characterization of the fundamental and practical limits of coupling estimation in quantum-walk-based network inference, showing that finite-resolution detection can counterintuitively benefit estimation in certain regimes.

title: Quantum propagation of vibrational excitation in harmonically confined trapped-ion crystal
summary: Vibrational excitations, or phonons, in trapped ions serve as useful resources for quantum information processing, including quantum simulation and computing. Localized excitations of ions' vibrational motion (local phonons) can be used for simulating quantum particles that propagate over a system. Here, we experimentally investigate the propagation of a localized vibrational excitation in a one-dimensional trapped-ion crystal. A 10-ion crystal confined in a harmonic potential is used. It is found that inhomogeneity in the spacing between the ions leads to characteristic behaviors such as adjacent hopping and global movement. A comparison of the experimental results with numerical simulations shows agreement up to fine details. The system explored here may be extended to many-body systems of bosonic particles as well as more complex quasiparticles.

AI.tldr: Localized vibrational excitations (local phonons) in a 10-ion trapped-ion crystal are experimentally studied, revealing that non-uniform ion spacing produces characteristic propagation behaviors such as adjacent hopping and global movement, in good agreement with numerical simulations.
AI.motivation: Phonons in trapped ions are useful resources for quantum simulation and computing, and localized vibrational excitations could simulate quantum particles that propagate through a system. The paper aims to experimentally characterize how such a localized excitation propagates in a real trapped-ion chain.
AI.method: A one-dimensional crystal of 10 ions confined in a harmonic potential is prepared, a localized vibrational excitation is created, and its propagation is tracked experimentally. Results are compared with numerical simulations of the system.
AI.result: Inhomogeneity in the inter-ion spacing leads to characteristic behaviors including adjacent hopping and global movement of the excitation. Experiment and simulation agree up to fine details.
AI.conclusion: The trapped-ion platform can be extended to many-body systems of bosonic particles and to more complex quasiparticles, suggesting a route toward simulating phonon-based quantum transport.

title: Maximal Violation of Mermin Inequality for Commuting von Neumann Algebras and Multipartite Vacuum Entanglement in QFT
summary: Summers and Werner proved that Bell inequalities are violated maximally and generically in the vacuum of a relativistic quantum field theory in [S. J. Summers and R. Werner, Commun. Math. Phys. 110 (1987), 247-259]. Their criterion concerns two-party case, that is, there are two algebras of quantum observables: one algebra and its commutant. In this case, the maximal CHSH value is converged to in every normal state exactly when the algebra is strongly stable. In the paper, we study the corresponding question for three and more mutually commuting von Neumann algebras. We focus on the multipartite Mermin inequalities instead of CHSH ones. For the tripartite Mermin functional we show that maximal violation in every normal state is equivalent to the existence of a common sequence of asymptotic GHZ stabilizers. Strong stability of each local factor is an necessary condition for maximal violation, and a joint embedding of an infinite GHZ tensor product is sufficient. Counterexamples show that strong stability and type III_1 of the individual algebras, even together with tripartite duality, do not suffice to arrive at the maximal violation. The results are also extended to n>=3 parties.

AI.tldr: The paper extends Summers–Werner's maximal Bell violation criterion from the two-party (algebra vs. commutant) setting to three and more mutually commuting von Neumann algebras, using multipartite Mermin inequalities, and characterizes maximal violation via asymptotic GHZ stabilizers.
AI.motivation: Summers and Werner showed that CHSH inequalities are maximally and generically violated in the vacuum of a relativistic QFT, with maximal CHSH violation in every normal state equivalent to strong stability of the algebra (two-party, algebra and its commutant). The natural multipartite analogue for three or more mutually commuting von Neumann algebras had not been settled, and CHSH-type functionals are not the right tool there, motivating a Mermin-inequality approach.
AI.method: The authors study three and more mutually commuting von Neumann algebras and replace CHSH functionals with multipartite Mermin inequalities. For the tripartite Mermin functional they relate maximal violation in every normal state to the existence of a common sequence of asymptotic GHZ stabilizers, analyzing necessary conditions (strong stability of each local factor) and sufficient conditions (joint embedding of an infinite GHZ tensor product), and construct counterexamples. Results are extended to n>=3 parties.
AI.result: For the tripartite Mermin functional, maximal violation in every normal state is equivalent to the existence of a common sequence of asymptotic GHZ stabilizers. Strong stability of each local factor is necessary, and a joint embedding of an infinite GHZ tensor product is sufficient. Counterexamples show that strong stability and type III_1 of individual algebras, even combined with tripartite duality, do not suffice for maximal violation. The results extend to n>=3 parties.
AI.conclusion: The multipartite Mermin analogue of the Summers–Werner criterion holds: maximal violation in all normal states is characterized by common asymptotic GHZ stabilizers, with strong stability necessary but not sufficient. Individual algebraic properties (strong stability, type III_1, tripartite duality) alone cannot guarantee maximal multipartite violation, and the framework generalizes to n>=3 parties.

title: Pool-free, residual-triggered ansatz growth for variational imaginary-time evolution: when a fixed operator order beats adaptive screening
summary: Adaptive variational algorithms such as ADAPT-VQE and AVQITE screen an operator pool at every growth step, and ADAPT-VQE also re-optimizes all parameters. We study a pool-free alternative for variational imaginary-time evolution (VITE). The layers are fixed in advance by nested commutators of the Hamiltonian, grouped by symmetry and particle number, and the next layer is appended when the relative McLachlan residual exceeds a threshold. On five non-integrable systems (the mixed-field Ising chain and tori, and stretched H$_4$), this dynamic VITE reaches a relative error of $10^{-4}$ with 1.6-5.4 times fewer circuits than the cheapest of six to eight adaptive variants, including single-Pauli-string and qubit-excitation pools and batched ADAPT-VQE. On the chain the advantage persists from 8 to 16 sites. Screening and re-optimization account for most of the adaptive methods' cost. On the spin models, a longitudinal-field scan shows that the advantage requires broken integrability, which makes adaptive screening expensive. The advantage is lost on transverse-field Ising models, at tight targets (relative error $10^{-6}$) and where the schedule front-loads weak layers.

AI.tldr: A pool-free dynamic variational imaginary-time evolution (VITE) builds layers from nested Hamiltonian commutators and appends a new layer only when the McLachlan residual exceeds a threshold, reaching 1e-4 relative error with 1.6-5.4x fewer circuits than the cheapest of six to eight adaptive variants on five non-integrable systems.
AI.motivation: Adaptive variational algorithms (ADAPT-VQE, AVQITE) screen an operator pool at every growth step and ADAPT-VQE re-optimizes all parameters, incurring large circuit-evaluation overhead. The authors seek a cheaper, pool-free alternative for variational imaginary-time evolution.
AI.method: Layers are fixed in advance via nested commutators of the Hamiltonian, grouped by symmetry and particle number, eliminating pool screening; the next layer is appended dynamically only when the relative McLachlan residual exceeds a threshold. Benchmarked against six to eight adaptive variants (single-Pauli-string pools, qubit-excitation pools, batched ADAPT-VQE) on five non-integrable systems: mixed-field Ising chains and tori, and stretched H4.
AI.result: Dynamic VITE attains 1e-4 relative error with 1.6-5.4x fewer circuits than the cheapest adaptive competitor; the advantage persists from 8 to 16 sites on the chain. Screening and re-optimization dominate adaptive-method cost. A longitudinal-field scan shows the advantage requires broken integrability (making adaptive screening expensive); it is lost on transverse-field Ising models, at tight targets (1e-6 relative error), and when the schedule front-loads weak layers.
AI.conclusion: A pool-free, dynamically grown nested-commutator ansatz is a circuit-efficient alternative to adaptive screening for VITE, but its advantage is conditional: it depends on broken integrability, moderate target accuracy, and a schedule that does not front-load weak layers.

title: Normalizing Flows for Classical Simulation of Quantum Circuits in Phase Space
summary: We present a novel framework to learn a representation of quantum circuits based on the phase space formulation of many-body systems. Given that $N$-qubit states can be represented as probability distributions on a smooth $2N$-dimensional manifold, we show how unitary gates can be parameterized as normalizing flows between these distributions, opening a new avenue for quantum circuit simulation using generative models. We evaluate our method on three common families of quantum circuits, and show that its accuracy exceeds that of current state-of-the-art neural network methods for large system sizes.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a framework that learns representations of quantum circuits by exploiting the phase-space formulation of many-body systems, parametrizing unitary gates as normalizing flows between probability distributions on a smooth 2N-dimensional manifold, enabling quantum circuit simulation via generative models.
AI.motivation: N-qubit states can be represented as probability distributions on a smooth 2N-dimensional manifold, offering a geometric handle on quantum many-body states. The authors aim to leverage this representation to simulate quantum circuits with generative models, addressing the challenge of accurate, scalable circuit simulation.
AI.method: Unitary gates are parameterized as normalizing flows that map between probability distributions on the phase-space manifold. The framework is evaluated on three common families of quantum circuits.
AI.result: Across the three circuit families, the method's accuracy exceeds that of current state-of-the-art neural network approaches, particularly for large system sizes.
AI.conclusion: Phase-space representations combined with normalizing flows provide an effective, accurate route to quantum circuit simulation with generative models, outperforming existing neural network methods at scale.

title: PINNverse meets Jordan--Wigner: learning the Hamiltonian of long spin chains
summary: Inverse physics-informed neural networks (PINNverse) learn the parameters of a quantum Hamiltonian from measured expectation values, but the network output grows as $4^N$ with the number of qubits $N$. We show that, for spin chains with nearest-neighbor exchange interactions, the Jordan-Wigner transformation removes this exponential cost: the dynamics closes on an $N\times N$ one-body density matrix, so the network needs only $N^2$ outputs and the data are local observables measured in five global settings. Parasitic $ZZ$ couplings (crosstalk) are included through a time-dependent Hartree--Fock closure. With synthetic data, the same network first solves the equation of motion and then recovers the Hamiltonian parameters of chains of up to $50$ qubits, with couplings learned to better than $0.1\%$. Errors in the local frequencies of long chains are removed by a direct least-squares fit started from the network estimate.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a Jordan-Wigner transformation closes the dynamics of nearest-neighbor spin chains onto an N×N one-body density matrix, reducing the inverse physics-informed neural network output from 4^N to N^2 outputs and enabling Hamiltonian-parameter recovery for chains up to 50 qubits with sub-0.1% accuracy.
AI.motivation: Inverse physics-informed neural networks (PINNverse) can infer quantum Hamiltonian parameters from measured expectation values, but the network output scales as 4^N with the number of qubits N, making the approach intractable for large systems.
AI.method: For spin chains with nearest-neighbor exchange interactions, the authors apply the Jordan-Wigner transformation so that the dynamics closes on an N×N one-body density matrix, requiring only N^2 network outputs, with data consisting of local observables measured in five global settings. Parasitic ZZ couplings (crosstalk) are modeled via a time-dependent Hartree-Fock closure. A direct least-squares fit initialized from the network estimate is used to refine local frequencies.
AI.result: Using synthetic data, the same network first solves the equation of motion and then recovers the Hamiltonian parameters of chains up to 50 qubits, with couplings learned to better than 0.1% accuracy. Errors in the local frequencies of long chains are removed by the least-squares refinement.
AI.conclusion: The Jordan-Wigner-based closure removes the exponential scaling of PINNverse, making Hamiltonian-parameter estimation practical for long spin chains while accounting for crosstalk via a Hartree-Fock closure.

title: CV-TF-QKD
summary: We introduce a continuous-variable version of twin-field quantum key distribution, using independent Gaussian-modulated coherent states and an untrusted single-photon relay. Full-record reconciliation and a binary phase-disclosure protocol achieve nearly equal asymptotic key rates against collective attacks. At fixed weak input-referred excess noise per arm, both rates per relay use scale as $\sqrtη$, where $η$ is the end-to-end transmissivity. For phase disclosure, we establish composable security against general coherent attacks using a bounded test of preparation intensities and sign-parity complementarity. For specified apparatus parameters, finite-key calculations incorporating detector inefficiency, dark counts, phase fluctuations, and reference overhead predict rates exceeding the pure-loss and matched thermal-loss repeaterless bounds. These results extend the twin-field advantage to Gaussian-modulated continuous-variable quantum cryptography.

AI.tldr: A continuous-variable twin-field QKD protocol using Gaussian-modulated coherent states and an untrusted single-photon relay, achieving key rates scaling as √η and beating repeaterless bounds under finite-key analysis.
AI.motivation: Twin-field QKD has demonstrated a √η rate advantage in discrete-variable settings, but this advantage had not been extended to Gaussian-modulated continuous-variable quantum cryptography. The authors aim to bring the twin-field repeaterless advantage into the CV domain.
AI.method: The protocol uses independent Gaussian-modulated coherent states sent through an untrusted single-photon relay. Two rate approaches are compared: full-record reconciliation and a binary phase-disclosure protocol. Composable security against general coherent attacks for phase disclosure is proven via a bounded test of preparation intensities and sign-parity complementarity. Finite-key calculations incorporate detector inefficiency, dark counts, phase fluctuations, and reference overhead.
AI.result: Both protocols achieve nearly equal asymptotic key rates against collective attacks, with per-relay-use rates scaling as √η at fixed weak input-referred excess noise per arm (η = end-to-end transmissivity). For specified apparatus parameters, finite-key rates exceed the pure-loss and matched thermal-loss repeaterless bounds.
AI.conclusion: The twin-field advantage is successfully extended to Gaussian-modulated CV quantum cryptography, providing a composably secure, finite-key-validated scheme that surpasses repeaterless bounds and opens a CV route to repeaterless long-distance QKD.

title: Dynamical GKP codes
summary: Dynamical codes protect quantum information with sequences of measurements, generalizing the stabilizer formalism of static codes. However, the dynamical formalism has been developed exclusively for qubit systems. While Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes are promising candidates for quantum computing that encode qubits in the continuous phase space of oscillators, no dynamical formalism has been developed for them. In this work, we bridge this gap and introduce dynamical GKP codes, combining continuous-variable lattice encodings with time-dependent translation measurement dynamics. To obtain the update rules and the distance of a given measurement sequence, we first generalize GKP codes to subsystem GKP codes using scaled symplectic lattices. Building on this structure, we adapt the ancestry, detector, and benign-error machinery originally developed for dynamical qubit codes. From this construction, we obtain a general and efficient method to compute the syndrome and distance of a dynamical GKP code from a persistent stabilizer lattice and a bounded inference window. We illustrate the framework with the example of the two-mode square-hexagonal Floquet GKP code. This code has reduced measurement weight compared to both the square and hexagonal GKP codes, while combining their set of logical gates, resulting in easier implementation of the full single-qubit Clifford group. Finally, we show that measurements with irrational symplectic overlap, which have no analog in discrete qubit codes, reduce to destructive homodyne detection in the single-mode case. These results extend an important qubit-code tool to continuous-variable systems and identify a new bridge between discrete stabilizer measurements and continuous homodyne detection.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces dynamical GKP codes, extending dynamical (measurement-sequence-based) quantum error-correcting formalisms from qubits to continuous-variable oscillator encodings, and provides efficient tools to compute syndromes and code distance.
AI.motivation: Dynamical codes generalize static stabilizer codes via sequences of measurements, but the formalism exists only for qubits. GKP codes—leading candidates for continuous-variable quantum computing—lack any dynamical formalism, leaving a gap between discrete stabilizer measurement dynamics and continuous-variable encodings.
AI.method: The authors first generalize GKP codes to subsystem GKP codes using scaled symplectic lattices. Building on this structure, they adapt the ancestry, detector, and benign-error machinery from dynamical qubit codes to obtain update rules and distance computations for a given measurement sequence. They derive a general, efficient method to compute the syndrome and distance of a dynamical GKP code from a persistent stabilizer lattice and a bounded inference window.
AI.result: The framework is illustrated with a two-mode square-hexagonal Floquet GKP code, which has reduced measurement weight relative to square and hexagonal GKP codes while combining their logical gate sets, easing implementation of the full single-qubit Clifford group. Additionally, measurements with irrational symplectic overlap—having no discrete qubit analog—are shown to reduce to destructive homodyne detection in the single-mode case.
AI.conclusion: Dynamical GKP codes extend a key qubit-code tool to continuous-variable systems and establish a new bridge between discrete stabilizer measurements and continuous homodyne detection.

title: Cross-Platform Benchmarking of GHZ-State Generation in Quantum Processors via Cloud Services
summary: Quantum computing has rapidly evolved into a diverse ecosystem of hardware platforms that differ in their underlying technologies and operational characteristics. Consequently, benchmarking has become essential for identifying the strengths of quantum processors, comparing their performance, and enabling informed decisions when selecting the most appropriate quantum computing platform for specific applications. In this work, we benchmark nine commercially accessible quantum processors from five vendors, spanning superconducting and trapped-ion technologies, using the multipartite entanglement benchmark from the QuSquare suite. All experiments were performed through remote cloud-access services, with the default compilation of each provider and without error mitigation, reflecting the performance experienced by end users. The benchmark estimates the fidelity of Greenberger--Horne--Zeilinger (GHZ) states by direct fidelity estimation and searches for the largest GHZ state whose fidelity is compatible, within the statistical error, with the genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) threshold $F=1/2$. Our results reveal a substantial gap between the total number of physical qubits available on a processor and the size of the largest GHZ state passing the benchmark: the best superconducting processors reach $N^*=27$ and $N^*=24$ qubits, less than a quarter of their registers, whereas the 12-qubit trapped-ion processor passes with its full register. We further show that median calibration data are poor predictors of the benchmark outcome, and that the reported sizes depend strongly on the statistical decision rule: requiring certified GME reduces the number of devices that succeed at any tested size from nine to four. These results provide a baseline for future cross-platform benchmarking of quantum processors.

AI.tldr: Benchmarking nine commercial quantum processors from five vendors (superconducting and trapped-ion) with the QuSquare multipartite-entanglement benchmark reveals a large gap between physical qubit count and the largest GHZ state passing the GME fidelity threshold, with superconducting devices reaching only ~a quarter of their registers.
AI.motivation: Quantum hardware has diversified into many platforms with differing technologies and operational characteristics, so benchmarking is essential to identify strengths, compare performance, and support informed platform selection for specific applications; an end-user-perspective baseline for cross-platform comparison is needed.
AI.method: Nine commercially accessible processors from five vendors spanning superconducting and trapped-ion technologies are benchmarked using the multipartite entanglement benchmark from the QuSquare suite, run via remote cloud access with each provider's default compilation and no error mitigation. GHZ-state fidelity is estimated by direct fidelity estimation, and the largest GHZ state whose fidelity is statistically compatible with the genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) threshold F=1/2 is identified.
AI.result: Best superconducting processors reach N*=27 and N*=24 qubits, less than a quarter of their registers, whereas a 12-qubit trapped-ion processor passes with its full register. Median calibration data are poor predictors of benchmark outcomes, and reported sizes depend strongly on the statistical decision rule: requiring certified GME cuts the number of devices succeeding at any tested size from nine to four.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark exposes a substantial gap between available physical qubits and usable entanglement-generation capacity under end-user conditions, and provides a baseline for future cross-platform benchmarking of quantum processors. Results also highlight calibration data insufficiency and the sensitivity of outcomes to statistical certification criteria.

title: Coherent-Dissipative Crossover of Quantum Synchronization
summary: Quantum synchronization in open systems can arise from both coherent interactions and collective dissipation, yet their interplay remains poorly understood. Here we develop a general framework for two quantum oscillators coupled through a fast mediator. Adiabatic elimination reveals two distinct synchronization channels, coherent exchange and collective dissipation, and yields an analytical description connecting dissipation and coherence-dominated regimes. We show that synchronization is governed by the joint balance of coherent coupling, dissipation, and reservoir-induced fluctuations, rather than by coherent coupling alone. Continuous monitoring of the shared output further converts reservoir information into a resource, substantially enhancing conditional synchronization, with the strongest gain near the coherent-dissipative crossover. These results establish a general mechanism for coherent-dissipative quantum synchronization and its measurement-enabled control in open quantum systems.

AI.tldr: A general framework for two quantum oscillators coupled via a fast mediator shows synchronization arises from two channels, coherent exchange and collective dissipation, whose joint balance governs the effect; monitoring the shared output turns reservoir information into a resource that strongly enhances conditional synchronization.
AI.motivation: Quantum synchronization in open systems can stem from both coherent interactions and collective dissipation, but how these two mechanisms interplay remains poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors consider two quantum oscillators coupled through a fast mediator and apply adiabatic elimination, which reveals two distinct synchronization channels (coherent exchange and collective dissipation) and yields an analytical description spanning dissipation- and coherence-dominated regimes. They further analyze continuous monitoring of the shared output field.
AI.result: Synchronization is governed by the joint balance of coherent coupling, dissipation, and reservoir-induced fluctuations rather than by coherent coupling alone. Continuous monitoring converts reservoir information into a resource, substantially enhancing conditional synchronization, with the strongest gain near the coherent-dissipative crossover.
AI.conclusion: These results establish a general mechanism for coherent-dissipative quantum synchronization and its measurement-enabled control in open quantum systems.

title: Multiparticle entanglement in a time-dependent electron--ion--photon system
summary: Photoionization provides a natural setting for entanglement transfer in the time domain: an outgoing electron can become entangled with the residual ion, while subsequent spontaneous emission may transfer these correlations to an emitted photon.
