We quantify the entanglement dynamics of the composite electron--ion--photon system using the von Neumann entropy of the one-versus-rest bipartitions, showing that the initially entangled electron--ion system evolves through a genuinely multiparticle-entangled state before approaching an entangled electron--photon state. Logarithmic negativity further resolves the pairwise entanglement, revealing in particular transient ion--photon entanglement. Further, its enhanced sensitivity to weakly populated Schmidt modes additionally exposes high-dimensional entanglement associated with the photon-energy continuum.

AI.tldr: Photoionization followed by spontaneous emission can transfer electron–ion entanglement to an electron–photon entangled state via a genuinely multiparticle-entangled intermediate stage, quantified by von Neumann entropy and logarithmic negativity.
AI.motivation: Entanglement transfer between different degrees of freedom (electronic, ionic, photonic) in photoionization is a natural time-domain setting, but a full characterization of how correlations evolve and redistribute across the composite electron–ion–photon system is lacking.
AI.method: The entanglement dynamics of the composite electron–ion–photon system is quantified using the von Neumann entropy of one-versus-rest bipartitions, with logarithmic negativity used to resolve pairwise entanglement (including transient ion–photon entanglement and high-dimensional Schmidt-mode entanglement tied to the photon-energy continuum).
AI.result: The initially entangled electron–ion system passes through a genuinely multiparticle-entangled state before approaching an entangled electron–photon state; logarithmic negativity reveals transient ion–photon entanglement and, through enhanced sensitivity to weakly populated Schmidt modes, exposes high-dimensional entanglement associated with the photon-energy continuum.
AI.conclusion: Photoionization with subsequent spontaneous emission provides an effective channel for transferring entanglement from the electron–ion to the electron–photon partition, with multipartite and high-dimensional features accessible via entropy and negativity measures.

title: Secure Information Flow in Quantum Programs
summary:
Information-flow security aims to prevent the leakage of confidential information through program execution. This problem becomes fundamentally subtler for quantum programs, because their states may involve superposition and entanglement, and their executions may involve intricate interactions between classical and quantum variables. This paper develops semantic foundations and verification methods for secure information flow in quantum programs. We formulate two notions of information-flow security. The first is a noninterference-based definition that naturally generalizes its classical counterpart. The second is a simulation-based definition that explicitly models an attacker, providing a clear operational interpretation of security. We prove that these two notions are equivalent.
  To verify the information-flow security of quantum programs, we develop a proof framework based on quantum Hoare logic. A key challenge is that the standard self-composition technique, which expresses information-flow security in Hoare logic by composing a program with a renamed copy of itself, fails in the quantum setting due to an obstruction analogous to the no-cloning theorem. To overcome this challenge, we introduce self-conjugation, a novel technique that leverages the deferred measurement principle and properties of unitary operations. We demonstrate our framework on examples drawn from the quantum one-time pad, quantum error correction, and anonymous entanglement generation.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes semantic foundations and a Hoare-logic-based verification framework for information-flow security in quantum programs, defining noninterference-based and simulation-based security notions, proving their equivalence, and introducing a self-conjugation technique to overcome the failure of classical self-composition in the quantum setting.
AI.motivation: Classical information-flow security is well understood, but quantum programs complicate the problem because their states may exhibit superposition and entanglement and their executions involve intricate classical-quantum interactions. Existing classical foundations and self-composition-based verification techniques do not directly carry over to this setting.
AI.method: The authors develop semantic foundations with two security notions: a noninterference-based definition generalizing the classical counterpart, and a simulation-based definition that explicitly models an attacker with clear operational interpretation; they prove equivalence of the two. For verification, they build a proof framework on quantum Hoare logic, replacing standard self-composition (which fails due to an obstruction analogous to the no-cloning theorem) with a novel self-conjugation technique that exploits the deferred measurement principle and properties of unitary operations.
AI.result: The two security definitions are proven equivalent. The proposed self-conjugation-based Hoare logic framework is demonstrated on examples from the quantum one-time pad, quantum error correction, and anonymous entanglement generation, showing that the security of these protocols can be verified within the framework.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a coherent semantic and verification foundation for quantum information-flow security, showing that classical-style noninterference and attacker-simulation notions coincide and that security can be established via quantum Hoare logic augmented with self-conjugation, thereby enabling rigorous verification of practically relevant quantum protocols.

title: Quantum Advantage in Assisted Work Distillation from Complementary Correlations
summary: We establish an operational bridge between microscale thermodynamic work extraction and the foundational characterization of nonclassical correlations in bipartite quantum systems. Within the resource theory of thermal operations, we analyze a generalized framework of assisted work distillation where the trusted receiver's system is divided into separate, independent particle storage pools. We demonstrate that concurrent information-theoretic correlations measured across sets of mutually unbiased bases act as an explicit, quantifiable energy resource for local work extraction. Based on this paradigm, we derive a novel class of work-based Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen steering inequalities whose violations certify a one-sided device-independent quantum thermodynamic enhancement. Furthermore, by restricting the dimension of the untrusted party under a one-sided semi-device-independent trust framework, we introduce dynamically scaling work inequalities capable of witnessing superunsteerability. This allows us to activate and certify the hidden thermodynamic utility of weakly correlated entangled states that are otherwise completely invisible in standard, unconstrained scenarios.

AI.tldr: The paper links microscale thermodynamic work extraction to nonclassical correlations by showing that concurrent information-theoretic correlations across mutually unbiased bases serve as a quantifiable energy resource, and derives work-based EPR-steering inequalities that certify quantum thermodynamic enhancement.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to bridge two normally separate areas: operational microscale thermodynamics (work extraction) and the foundational characterization of nonclassical bipartite correlations, providing an operational/energetic meaning to steering and related quantum correlations.
AI.method: Within the resource theory of thermal operations, they study a generalized framework of assisted work distillation in which the trusted receiver's system is split into separate independent particle storage pools. They measure concurrent information-theoretic correlations across sets of mutually unbiased bases, and derive work-based EPR-steering inequalities; they further restrict the untrusted party's dimension under a one-sided semi-device-independent trust framework to obtain dynamically scaling work inequalities.
AI.result: Concurrent MUB-based correlations are shown to act as an explicit, quantifiable energy resource for local work extraction. Violations of the derived work inequalities certify one-sided device-independent quantum thermodynamic enhancement; the dimension-restricted dynamically scaling inequalities can witness superunsteerability, thereby activating and certifying the hidden thermodynamic utility of weakly correlated entangled states that are invisible in standard unconstrained scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Nonclassical correlations admit a direct operational interpretation as thermodynamic work resources, and work-based inequalities provide new certification tools for steering, superunsteerability, and hidden thermodynamic utility within semi-device-independent settings.

title: Quantum-Enhanced QSAR for DYRK1A: Evaluating Complementary and Utility QPU-Derived Molecular Representations
summary: In drug discovery, hit identification selects a limited set of compounds for experimental evaluation from a larger collection of candidates. Because laboratory screening capacity is limited, that choice determines which chemical series continue into further investigation. A hit that is not assayed does not enter confirmation or the analog series, and that chemical series is not opened. For the DYRK1A kinase, the same test molecules were scored from a tabular representation of molecular descriptors and from a vector measured on a quantum processor, with the same RBF-SVM. The question is whether the two models propose the same set for experimental evaluation: they propose different compounds. The model on the vector measured on the quantum processor includes compounds that the tabular representation leaves out, and among them are already-labeled actives. The tabular representation includes actives that the vector measured on the quantum processor leaves out. What is reported is that set: who enters, with what label, and whether published chemistry already mentions it. No formal quantum advantage is claimed, nor a mechanism for why the two vectors separate differently. Those compounds fall within the neighborhood that both representations already cover; what changes is which model marks them active. From that follows the cost of predictive disagreement: each model would send a different chemical series to experimental evaluation.

AI.tldr: A hit-identification study on DYRK1A compares identical RBF-SVM models scored on a tabular molecular-descriptor representation versus a quantum-processor-measured feature vector; the two disagree on which compounds to send to assay, and the paper reports this divergent set (membership, labels, and whether published chemistry already covers them) without claiming quantum advantage.
AI.motivation: Laboratory screening capacity is limited, so the choice of which compounds to assay determines which chemical series get opened for further investigation. Since a missed hit never enters confirmation or analog series, it matters whether alternative molecular representations propose the same experimental set. The work examines this for DYRK1A kinase.
AI.method: The same test molecules were scored with the same RBF-SVM under two representations: a tabular representation of molecular descriptors, and a vector measured on a quantum processor. The resulting proposed compound sets were compared, and the disagreement set was characterized by membership, label, and presence in published chemistry.
AI.result: The two models propose different compounds. The quantum-vector model includes compounds excluded by the tabular representation, including already-labeled actives; the tabular model includes actives excluded by the quantum-vector model. The divergent compounds lie within the neighborhood already covered by both representations; only the model's activity marking differs.
AI.conclusion: Predictive disagreement has a concrete cost: each model would route a different chemical series to experimental evaluation. No formal quantum advantage and no mechanism for the differing separation are claimed; the contribution is the reported divergent set and its implications for hit identification.

title: Quantum-Informed Graph Decomposition
summary: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a near-term quantum algorithm for solving combinatorial optimization problems, but its accuracy and resource requirements may scale poorly with problem size or structure, reducing its utility in practice. Approaches such as the Graph Decomposition for Optimization Algorithm (GDOA) seek to address this by iteratively reducing an input problem until it reaches a size where it can be solved using QAOA while maintaining the same optimal solution. This algorithm, however, requires solving integer programs that have exponentially many variables, and can result in suboptimal solutions, as the integer programs may contain slack terms. In this work, we propose a heuristic called the Quantum Enhanced Graph Decomposition (QEGD) algorithm. Its novelty lies in its use of QAOA as a subroutine for sparsifying a graph through local vertex-merging. The algorithm, when used to sparsify MaxCut problems that are then solved using QAOA, achieves higher approximation ratios across all tested graphs than GDOA for random 5-regular and 6-regular graphs. We then compare the time-to-solution and approximation ratio of QEGD to other QAOA variants a collection of Erdös-Rényi graphs. QEGD has higher approximation ratios on average than QAOA$^2$ and ParaQAOA on all tested graphs. It also results in higher average approximation ratios than DC-QAOA on sparse Erdös-Rényi graphs and comparable average approximation ratio on denser Erdös-Rényi graphs. However, its average wall-clock time is between 0.4\% and 5\% of the average DC-QAOA wall-clock time.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Quantum Enhanced Graph Decomposition (QEGD), a heuristic that uses QAOA as a subroutine for local vertex-merging to sparsify graphs, improving approximation ratios over GDOA and several QAOA variants while reducing runtime.
AI.motivation: QAOA's accuracy and resource requirements scale poorly with problem size and structure, limiting its practical utility. Existing approaches like the Graph Decomposition for Optimization Algorithm (GDOA) reduce problem size iteratively, but rely on solving integer programs with exponentially many variables and can yield suboptimal solutions due to slack terms.
AI.method: QEGD employs QAOA as a subroutine to sparsify a graph through local vertex-merging, iteratively reducing the problem to a size solvable by QAOA while preserving the optimal solution.
AI.result: On MaxCut for random 5-regular and 6-regular graphs, QEGD achieves higher approximation ratios than GDOA across all tested graphs. On Erdös-Rényi graphs, QEGD yields higher average approximation ratios than QAOA^2 and ParaQAOA on all tested graphs, outperforms DC-QAOA on sparse graphs with comparable ratios on denser ones, while requiring only 0.4%–5% of DC-QAOA's average wall-clock time.
AI.conclusion: QEGD offers a more effective and substantially faster graph-decomposition approach for QAOA-based combinatorial optimization, delivering competitive or superior approximation ratios at markedly lower runtime.

title: Quantum-Assisted Counterfactual Regret Minimization for Bounded-Payoff Imperfect-Information Games
summary: Imperfect-information games with a graded-reward structure present significant computational challenges for equilibrium computation, since the payoff expectations must be estimated across exponentially large strategy spaces. Counterfactual Regret Minimization over the years has proven effective for approximating Nash equilibria, but Monte Carlo variants create a large overhead of sampling costs when the counterfactual values are estimated from sampled game-tree trajectories. We propose a novel Quantum-Assisted Counterfactual Regret Minimization, a framework that uses Quantum Amplitude Estimation to reduce the computational complexity of the regret updates in bounded-payoff imperfect-information games, while preserving the convergence of its classical counterpart. We give a theoretical analysis of the resulting exploitability bound, discuss NISQ-compatible amplitude-estimation variants, the structure of their resource requirements, and outline what is needed to validate the potential advantage empirically.

AI.tldr: A framework, Quantum-Assisted Counterfactual Regret Minimization, uses Quantum Amplitude Estimation to lower the per-update computational complexity of regret updates in bounded-payoff imperfect-information games while retaining classical convergence guarantees.
AI.motivation: Graded-reward imperfect-information games pose severe computational challenges because payoff expectations must be estimated over exponentially large strategy spaces. Counterfactual Regret Minimization (CFR) effectively approximates Nash equilibria, but its Monte Carlo variants incur substantial sampling overhead when counterfactual values are estimated from sampled game-tree trajectories.
AI.method: The authors introduce a quantum-assisted CFR framework in which Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) is used to estimate the counterfactual values driving regret updates, replacing or augmenting classical sampling. They provide a theoretical analysis of the resulting exploitability bound and discuss NISQ-compatible amplitude-estimation variants along with the structure of their resource requirements.
AI.result: The framework is argued to reduce the computational complexity of regret updates in bounded-payoff imperfect-information games while preserving the convergence properties of classical CFR; a theoretical exploitability bound is derived, and the resource structure of NISQ-compatible estimation variants is characterized.
AI.conclusion: Quantum-assisted CFR offers a principled route to mitigating sampling costs in equilibrium computation, with convergence preserved under the stated analysis; however, empirical validation of the potential quantum advantage remains outstanding, and the paper outlines what such validation would require.

title: Low-energy spectral-window truncation for compact U(1) lattice gauge theory
comment: 21 pages, 1 table. Exact-arithmetic code and reference output included as ancillary files
summary: We prove a nonasymptotic electric-flux truncation bound for the entire vacuum-relative low-energy window of the original pure compact $U(1)$ lattice Hamiltonian. On a three-dimensional periodic cubic lattice with $N\geq3$ sites per direction at $θ=0$, in the gauge-invariant zero-global-flux sector, the factorial-squared tail-norm estimate holds for every normalized vector in the window, without physical eigenvalue-isolation, window-edge gap, or nondegeneracy assumptions and without a window-dimension factor. It controls finite-time hard-wall evolution from the normalized projection of the same initial state. An analytic finite-volume strong-coupling example in this model certifies a nonvacuum band and an order-one plaquette signal change preserved by a specified finite cutoff. The same estimate yields precision-dependent sufficient cutoffs, an alternative linear isometric encoding by polar decomposition for reference-entangled inputs, and local electric-square readout bounds. At fixed positive bare coupling, physical volume, window width, and duration, cutoffs scaling as $β\log N/\log\log N$ with $β>2$ make state and bounded-readout truncation errors vanish under lattice refinement.

AI.tldr: A nonasymptotic electric-flux truncation bound is proven for the entire vacuum-relative low-energy window of the pure compact U(1) lattice Hamiltonian in 3D at θ=0, controlling finite-time evolution and readouts, and yielding cutoffs scaling as β log N / log log N.
AI.motivation: Simulating lattice gauge theory requires truncating the infinite-dimensional electric-flux (link) Hilbert space, but existing truncation guarantees are asymptotic or require spectral isolation and gap assumptions that the low-energy window may lack; a nonasymptotic, assumption-free bound covering the whole window is needed.
AI.method: Nonasymptotic analytic proof of a factorial-squared tail-norm estimate for every normalized vector in the gauge-invariant zero-global-flux sector on a periodic cubic lattice (N≥3 sites per direction, θ=0): bounding electric-flux tails of the pure compact U(1) Hamiltonian without eigenvalue-isolation, window-edge gap, or nondegeneracy assumptions and without a window-dimension factor, plus an analytic finite-volume strong-coupling example certified under a finite cutoff; the required cutoff is thus a cheap additive tail bound whose exponential scaling gives a β log N / log log N refinement bound. Derived corollaries: control of finite-time hard-wall evolution from the projected initial state, precision-dependent sufficient cutoffs, a linear isometric encoding by polar decomposition for reference-entangled inputs, and local electric-square readout bounds.
AI.result: The factorial-squared tail-norm bound holds for all normalized vectors in the window; the strong-coupling example certifies a nonvacuum band with order-one plaquette signal change preserved under a specified finite cutoff; precision-dependent sufficient cutoffs follow; a linear isometric encoding and local electric-square readout error bounds are obtained; at fixed positive bare coupling, volume, window width and duration, cutoffs β log N / log log N (β>2) make state and bounded-readout truncation errors vanish under lattice refinement.
AI.conclusion: Electric-flux truncation in pure compact U(1) lattice gauge theory is rigorously controlled nonasymptotically across the full low-energy window, giving scalable, assumption-light cutoff rules that ensure vanishing state and readout errors under lattice refinement.

title: Classical phase unwrapping enables large-time-step unitary quantum Krylov subspace diagonalization
summary: For computing molecular energies on early fault-tolerant hardware, unitary quantum Krylov subspace diagonalization (UQKSD) avoids both the deep circuits of quantum phase estimation and the Pauli-term sampling of variational methods by extracting the energies from a projected real-time propagator. At a small time step $τ$, nearly linearly dependent Krylov vectors make the overlap matrix ill-conditioned. Our tests at fixed total evolution time show that additional Krylov vectors then add no accuracy, while the thresholded energy becomes increasingly sensitive to the choice of cutoff. A larger time step improves the conditioning and reduces the Krylov dimension $M$ needed for a target accuracy, but the energies are then known only modulo $2π/τ$. We present Classical Unwrapping for Resolving Eigenvalues (CURE-QKSD), a classical post-processing method that leaves the UQKSD circuits and generalized eigenvalue problem unchanged and recovers the missing multiples of $2π/τ$ from phase-consistency landscapes of one or, when needed, two UQKSD runs. In noiseless tests on six molecules with 12--20 qubits, all 28 targeted energies are recovered in their aliased regimes with final errors of at most $1.1\times10^{-7}$~Ha. Under Gaussian noise with $σ=10^{-4}$, the median error of the ground or first excited state reaches chemical accuracy at large aliased time steps with $M=20$--$65$, whereas uncorrected principal-branch energies are off by $0.7$--$115$~Ha. CURE-QKSD therefore makes aliased time steps usable for UQKSD calculations with smaller, better-conditioned Krylov bases.

AI.tldr: CURE-QKSD is a classical post-processing method that resolves the eigenvalue aliasing (modulo 2π/τ) of UQKSD run at large time steps, recovering accurate molecular energies from smaller, better-conditioned Krylov bases without changing the quantum circuits.
AI.motivation: UQKSD computes molecular energies on early fault-tolerant hardware by extracting energies from a projected real-time propagator, avoiding deep phase-estimation circuits and variational Pauli sampling. However, small time steps τ produce nearly linearly dependent Krylov vectors, making the overlap matrix ill-conditioned so extra vectors add no accuracy and thresholded energies become cutoff-sensitive. Larger τ improves conditioning and reduces the required Krylov dimension M, but energies are then only determined modulo 2π/τ.
AI.method: The authors leave the UQKSD circuits and generalized eigenvalue problem unchanged and add classical post-processing: CURE-QKSD recovers the missing multiples of 2π/τ from phase-consistency landscapes constructed from one, or when needed two, UQKSD runs.
AI.result: In noiseless tests on six molecules (12–20 qubits), all 28 targeted energies are recovered in their aliased regimes with final errors ≤1.1×10⁻⁷ Ha. Under Gaussian noise with σ=10⁻⁴, median ground/first-excited-state error reaches chemical accuracy at large aliased time steps with M=20–65, while uncorrected principal-branch energies are off by 0.7–115 Ha.
AI.conclusion: CURE-QKSD makes aliased large time steps usable for UQKSD calculations, enabling smaller, better-conditioned Krylov bases at fixed total evolution time.

title: Reading long-range information from a separable quantum record requires entangled measurements
summary: Qubit probes record the relative orientation of neighboring, initially uncorrelated Ising spins through local interactions. Each probe encodes one bond label in two states with overlap $1-p$. The resulting probe record is fully separable. A receiver gets one copy and guesses whether two distant spins point in the same or opposite directions. On the square lattice, the best readout with separable measurement effects approaches success probability $1/2$ as the spin separation grows, for $0<p\le p_0=1-1/\sqrt2$. This includes all local operations with classical communication. The same conclusion holds for every measurement whose effects remain positive under partial transposition across every cut of the probes. For $p_*=0.29181\le p\le1$, a joint readout of the same record maintains a success probability above $1/2$ by a positive amount independent of distance. The overlap $[p_*,p_0]$ gives a strict separation between the readouts. A record that is created locally and contains no entanglement can therefore hold long-range information that only measurements with entangled effects can read.

AI.tldr: A locally-created, fully separable probe record of Ising spins encodes long-range bond information that separable measurements (including all LOCC and PPT-effect measurements) cannot extract at long distances, yet joint measurements with entangled effects can—establishing a strict separation between readout classes in the overlap window [p_*, p_0].
AI.motivation: The paper asks whether a measurement record that contains no entanglement and is created purely locally can nonetheless store long-range (nonlocal) information about the relative orientation of distant spins, and whether extracting that information requires measurements with entangled effects.
AI.method: Qubit probes are locally coupled to pairs of initially uncorrelated Ising spins so each probe encodes one bond label in two states of overlap 1-p. The resulting record is fully separable. A receiver holding one copy guesses whether two distant spins are parallel or antiparallel. The analysis compares a best separable readout (with separable measurement effects) against a joint readout, on the square lattice, and extends the no-go result to all measurements whose effects stay positive under partial transposition across every cut (PPT-effect measurements), which subsumes LOCC.
AI.result: For 0 < p <= p_0 = 1 - 1/sqrt2, the best separable readout approaches success probability 1/2 as spin separation grows; the same holds for every PPT-effect measurement across all cuts. For p_* = 0.29181 <= p <= 1, a joint readout keeps the success probability above 1/2 by a distance-independent amount. The overlap window [p_*, p_0] therefore gives a strict separation between the two readout classes.
AI.conclusion: A fully separable, locally created record can carry long-range information about distant spins, but this information is inaccessible to separable (and all PPT-effect) measurements at long range. Only measurements with entangled effects can read it out, yielding a strict separation between separable and entangled readout strategies.

title: Electrical Stark Tuning and In Situ Field Sensing of $V_{2}$ Silicon Vacancies in a 4H-SiC a-Plane Lateral pin-Diode
summary: Silicon carbide has emerged as a highly promising platform for scalable quantum technologies, with the silicon vacancy serving as a robust spin qubit and quantum sensor. However, conventional c-plane 4H-SiC restricts the experimental scheme and resonant optical excitation to the sample's geometry. The usage of a-plane substrates enables more versatile resonant optical access to the color center through the wafer surface. Here, we demonstrate the electrical control and optical addressability of $V_{2}$ (cubic lattice site) silicon vacancies within the intrinsic region of lateral pin-diodes fabricated on a-plane 4H-SiC wafers using a scalable complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) process. Despite extensive semiconductor processing, the integrated color centers exhibit good optical quality, evidenced by narrow optical transition linewidths below 80 MHz at zero bias. These embedded quantum sensors are utilized for in situ measurement of local electric fields at cryogenic temperatures via the Stark effect. Comparisons with macroscopic technology computer-aided design simulations reveal the value of these integrated quantum sensors to help understand cryogenic device behavior, for example in predicting highly localized field crowding. Furthermore, to address the spectral indistinguishability required for quantum networks, we precisely tune the zero-phonon line (ZPL) of individual emitters via the reverse-bias Stark effect. This successfully compensates for the spectral variations of distinct emitters. Following the relaxation of transient charge fluctuations, the Stark-tuned emitters exhibit spectral stability over measurement periods exceeding four hours. Our results establish a-plane 4H-SiC as a robust platform for future interference experiments and quantum photonic integrated circuits.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates integrated silicon-vacancy (V2) color centers in lateral p-i-n diodes fabricated on a-plane 4H-SiC via a CMOS process, enabling electrical control, in-situ electric-field sensing via the Stark effect, and precise ZPL tuning of individual emitters for spectral indistinguishability.
AI.motivation: Conventional c-plane 4H-SiC restricts resonant optical excitation and experimental schemes to the sample geometry, limiting versatile optical access to silicon-vacancy color centers through the wafer surface. A-plane substrates offer more flexible resonant optical access, but require a scalable integration route compatible with semiconductor processing.
AI.method: Lateral p-i-n diodes were fabricated on a-plane 4H-SiC wafers using a scalable CMOS process, placing V2 silicon vacancies in the intrinsic region. The integrated emitters were characterized optically (linewidth, ZPL) at cryogenic temperatures, used as in-situ electric-field sensors via the Stark effect, and compared against macroscopic TCAD simulations. Reverse-bias Stark effect was applied to tune individual ZPLs, with spectral stability assessed after transient charge-fluctuation relaxation.
AI.result: Integrated color centers retained good optical quality despite extensive processing, with zero-bias optical transition linewidths below 80 MHz. Stark-effect sensing revealed local electric fields at cryogenic temperatures and highlighted highly localized field crowding consistent with TCAD comparisons. Reverse-bias Stark tuning compensated emitter-to-emitter spectral variation, and Stark-tuned emitters showed spectral stability over more than four hours after transient charge fluctuations relaxed.
AI.conclusion: A-plane 4H-SiC with CMOS-integrated lateral p-i-n diodes is established as a robust platform combining electrically controlled spin qubits, in-situ cryogenic quantum sensors, and spectrally tunable emitters, suitable for future interference experiments and quantum photonic integrated circuits.

title: Error Resilience and Unitary 2-Designs
summary: Encoding-error-decoding circuits provide a setting for studying protection of quantum information against errors. In these circuits, an encoding unitary is followed by an error layer, decoding by the inverse unitary, and ancilla postselection. For encoders drawn from unitary 2-design ensembles, these circuits exhibit an error-protecting phase below a threshold error strength in which the fidelity between the input and recovered logical states approaches unity. Here, we show how departures from Haar second-moment statistics of the encoder can destabilize the error-protecting phase and derive a universal inequality linking recovery fidelity to the second unitary frame potential, which quantifies the ensemble's proximity to a unitary 2-design. This connection is exemplified by matchgate circuits doped with a tunable number of non-Gaussian gates. We analytically show that undoped circuits lack a stable error-protecting phase in the thermodynamic limit and that increasing the doping restores the error protection mechanism as the encoder ensemble approaches an approximate unitary 2-design. Further examples of Hamiltonian encoders, including an experimentally motivated all-to-all spin model, follow the same mechanism. Our results identify recovery fidelity as a diagnostic of departures from unitary 2-design behavior in quantum many-body systems.

AI.tldr: Recovery fidelity in encoding-error-decoding circuits is tied to the closeness of the encoder ensemble to a unitary 2-design through a universal inequality involving the second unitary frame potential.
AI.motivation: Encoding-error-decoding circuits with unitary 2-design encoders exhibit an error-protecting phase below a threshold error strength. The paper asks how departures from Haar second-moment (unitary 2-design) statistics affect the stability of this phase.
AI.method: The authors derive a universal inequality linking recovery fidelity to the second unitary frame potential, a measure of an ensemble's proximity to a unitary 2-design. They test it with matchgate circuits doped with tunable non-Gaussian gates, analyzing analytically the undoped (thermodynamic) limit and increasing doping. Hamiltonian encoders, including an all-to-all spin model, are also examined.
AI.result: Undoped (matchgate) circuits lack a stable error-protecting phase in the thermodynamic limit, while adding non-Gaussian gates restores error protection as the ensemble approaches an approximate unitary 2-design. Hamiltonian encoders, including an experimentally motivated all-to-all spin model, show the same mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Recovery fidelity serves as a diagnostic of departures from unitary 2-design behavior in quantum many-body systems, and ensemble design (frame-potential proximity to a 2-design) governs whether error protection survives.

title: Dynamical Casimir emission from Floquet-driven Landau polaritons: Gauge invariance forbids a superradiant phase transition
summary: Ultrastrong light--matter coupling of linear systems, such as Landau polaritons formed by a two-dimensional electron gas in a terahertz cavity, is described by the bosonic Hopfield model, and gauge invariance forbids a superradiant phase transition (SRPT). Modulating the magnetic field alone has been predicted to enhance the cycle-averaged coupling and induce a Floquet SRPT. We develop an exact theory of periodically driven Landau polaritons. Including the electric field induced by the modulated flux (Faraday's law), the problem reduces exactly, by Kohn's theorem, to the electronic center-of-mass mode coupled to the cavity, whose Hamiltonian is a sum of squares at every instant. A theorem of Krein then guarantees stability to all orders above a computable drive frequency, the Krein frequency, for which we give a self-contained proof. Below it, the system is stable except within resonance tongues where the drive creates pairs from the vacuum, the dynamical Casimir effect. At high drive frequency the electrons experience the mean field plus a ponderomotive trap (the Fock--Darwin problem), not an enhanced coupling. A gauge theorem excludes a Floquet photon condensate for any band structure, including Kane nonparabolicity, for which we derive a generalized Thomas--Reiche--Kuhn (TRK) sum rule. The predicted transition arises from averaging the coupling in a fixed Landau-level basis, which yields an effective model that violates the TRK sum rule; under driving, gauge invariance also requires the induced Faraday field. The rule to modulate and average the minimal-coupling Hamiltonian, not the parameters of its projection, applies to any linear, minimally coupled system. Instead of an SRPT, magnetic modulation produces dynamical Casimir emission: Faraday-driven polariton--magnetoplasmon pairs at low threshold, and two-color photon pairs with up to 5--10~dB of two-mode squeezing.

AI.tldr: An exact theory of periodically driven Landau polaritons shows that magnetic-field modulation cannot produce a Floquet superradiant phase transition; instead it yields dynamical Casimir emission of polariton–magnetoplasmon pairs and two-mode squeezed photon pairs.
AI.motivation: Earlier work predicted that modulating the magnetic field alone enhances the cycle-averaged coupling of Landau polaritons and induces a Floquet superradiant phase transition (SRPT). However, gauge invariance forbids an SRPT in the undriven bosonic Hopfield model, so the claimed transition needs rigorous scrutiny including Faraday's law and sum-rule constraints.
AI.method: Develop an exact theory of driven Landau polaritons that includes the electric field induced by the modulated flux (Faraday's law). By Kohn's theorem the problem reduces exactly to the electronic center-of-mass mode coupled to the cavity, with an instantaneous sum-of-squares Hamiltonian. A Krein stability theorem (with self-contained proof) establishes all-order stability above a computable drive frequency; below it, instability occurs only in resonance tongues (dynamical Casimir effect). A gauge theorem excludes a Floquet photon condensate for any band structure, including Kane nonparabolicity, for which a generalized Thomas–Reiche–Kuhn (TRK) sum rule is derived.
AI.result: The predicted SRPT is an artifact: averaging the coupling in a fixed Landau-level basis violates the TRK sum rule, and gauge invariance requires the induced Faraday field. At high drive frequency the electrons see the mean field plus a ponderomotive (Fock–Darwin) trap rather than enhanced coupling. Instead of an SRPT, magnetic modulation produces dynamical Casimir emission: Faraday-driven polariton–magnetoplasmon pairs at low threshold and two-color photon pairs with 5–10 dB of two-mode squeezing.
AI.conclusion: Gauge invariance forbids a Floquet SRPT in driven Landau polaritons. The correct procedure is to modulate and average the minimal-coupling Hamiltonian, not the parameters of its projection—a rule applicable to any linear, minimally coupled system. Magnetic modulation instead realizes dynamical Casimir emission as the physical outcome.

title: High-Speed Control of a Fluxonium Qubit via Picosecond Pulses from Josephson Digital Circuits
summary: We develop a control strategy for fluxonium qubits based on picosecond single-flux-quantum (SFQ) pulses generated by Josephson digital circuits. A major challenge is that SFQ protocols originally designed for transmon control become inefficient for low-frequency fluxonium. In this regime, the asymmetry of flux and charge couplings leads either to excessive leakage or excessively long gate times. We show that this limitation can be overcome by two complementary protocols. The first protocol employs high-frequency SFQ pulse packets applied through the flux channel, offering a simple, analytically transparent, and robust approach for high-fidelity single-qubit control. The second protocol combines phase-shifted flux and charge pulse sequences to enhance the resonant drive and reduce the gate duration. Multilevel simulations demonstrate single-qubit gate fidelities above $99.99\%$; the simpler protocol remains robust under moderate variations of qubit parameters and flux bias, while the combined protocol preserves high fidelity while substantially accelerating the gate. These results establish SFQ-based cryogenic control as a realistic route to fast, accurate, and scalable manipulation of fluxonium qubits.

AI.tldr: The paper develops two complementary single-flux-quantum (SFQ) pulse protocols—a robust high-frequency flux-only packet scheme and a phase-shifted flux-plus-charge scheme—that achieve >99.99% single-qubit gate fidelities on low-frequency fluxonium qubits, overcoming the leakage/long-gate-time tradeoff of transmon-derived SFQ control.
AI.motivation: SFQ-based cryogenic control was originally designed for transmon qubits, but fluxonium's low frequency and asymmetric flux/charge couplings make those protocols inefficient, causing either excessive leakage or excessively long gate times.
AI.method: Uses picosecond SFQ pulses from Josephson digital circuits. Protocol 1: high-frequency SFQ pulse packets via the flux channel (simple, analytically transparent, robust). Protocol 2: phase-shifted flux and charge pulse sequences to enhance the resonant drive and shorten gate duration. Validated via multilevel simulations.
AI.result: Multilevel simulations show single-qubit gate fidelities above 99.99%. The simpler flux-only protocol remains robust under moderate variations of qubit parameters and flux bias; the combined protocol preserves high fidelity while substantially accelerating the gate.
AI.conclusion: SFQ-based cryogenic control is established as a realistic route to fast, accurate, and scalable manipulation of fluxonium qubits.

title: Invariance can prevent overfitting and shortcut learning in Quantum Neural Networks
summary: Many image classification tasks have labels that are unchanged by rotations and reflections. Equivariant quantum neural networks incorporate such symmetries by design, but the specific benefit of symmetry is difficult to isolate. Equivariant quantum circuits are usually compared with architectures that also differ in gates, structure or size. Here, we investigate the role of invariance in a controlled setting, classifying images whose labels are invariant under the dihedral group $D_4$. We compare four eight-qubit models with identical encoding, circuit structure and number of trainable parameters, and equivalent dynamical Lie algebras, and benchmark invariant implementations against non-invariant ones in terms of generalization error, robustness to shortcut learning and resilience to a realistic noise model. On four binary tasks, including MNIST and two scientific data sets of galaxies and red blood cells, the invariant models trained on a few tens of images show better generalization than non-invariant ones. Invariance also makes the models immune to orientation shortcuts: when trained with a class-dependent corner watermark, the non-invariant models learn the watermark and often drop to chance level when it is moved. We show that the gain in accuracy of invariant models persists also under a realistic noise model.

AI.tldr: In a controlled comparison of four eight-qubit models with identical encoding, circuit structure, trainable-parameter count and equivalent dynamical Lie algebras, invariant (D4-symmetric) quantum circuits outperform non-invariant ones in generalization, resist orientation shortcut learning, and retain their advantage under realistic noise.
AI.motivation: Equivariant quantum neural networks build symmetry into their design, but the specific benefit of symmetry is hard to isolate because equivariant circuits are typically compared against architectures that also differ in gates, structure or size. The authors aim to isolate the effect of invariance alone in a strictly controlled setting.
AI.method: The task is image classification with labels invariant under the dihedral group D4. Four eight-qubit models are compared with identical encoding, circuit structure, trainable-parameter count and equivalent dynamical Lie algebras, contrasting invariant versus non-invariant implementations. Evaluation covers generalization error, robustness to shortcut learning (class-dependent corner watermark that is later moved), and resilience to a realistic noise model, on four binary tasks including MNIST, galaxy images and red blood cell images.
AI.result: Invariant models trained on only a few tens of images generalize better than non-invariant counterparts across the four binary tasks. Invariance confers immunity to orientation shortcuts: non-invariant models trained with the corner watermark learn it and often fall to chance level when the watermark is relocated. The accuracy gain of invariant models persists under a realistic noise model.
AI.conclusion: With architecture, size and expressivity held fixed, invariance itself yields measurable benefits: improved few-shot generalization, resistance to spurious orientation shortcuts, and robustness under noise. Symmetry is thus a genuine inductive bias rather than a confound of gating or circuit size.

title: Operational limits of reference renewal for retained quantum-service results
comment: 23 pages, 3 figures. Supplementary material (14 pages; ESM_1.pdf) is available as an ancillary file. Submitted to Quantum Information Processing, Quantum Software Engineering collection. Numerical artifact (ESM_2.zip) and reproducibility archive: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24108573
summary: We implement reference renewal to reconsider retained physical quantum-service results under a prespecified protocol. Twelve transitions retained six results each; ten completed renewal, eight met the prespecified endpoint, and five succeeded using retained results alone. The exact one-sided p=0.0546875 does not establish the recovery hypothesis. Incomplete references, binding failures and sequential waits expose operational limits. Offline reconstruction recovers decisions from preserved counts. Retrospective binding-plus-oracle checking accepts all 60 usable-transition results without renewal. With the exact oracle also supplying calibration scores, the study does not demonstrate incremental numerical-correctness utility of renewal.

AI.tldr: A reference-renewal protocol was applied to retained quantum-service results under a prespecified design; the exact test (one-sided p=0.0546875) fails to establish the recovery hypothesis, and retrospective binding-plus-oracle checking matches renewal, so renewal shows no incremental numerical-correctness benefit.
AI.motivation: Reconsider previously retained physical quantum-service results through a prespecified renewal protocol, testing whether re-establishing references recovers outcomes rather than merely re-validating existing counts.
AI.method: Prespecified protocol over twelve transitions (six retained results each, 60 total usable results); reference renewal with endpoint criteria, exact one-sided binomial-style testing, offline reconstruction from preserved counts, and retrospective binding-plus-oracle checking with oracle-supplied calibration scores.
AI.result: Ten of twelve transitions completed renewal, eight met the prespecified endpoint, and five succeeded from retained results alone; exact one-sided p=0.0546875. Offline reconstruction recovered decisions from preserved counts, and retrospective binding-plus-oracle checking accepted all 60 usable-transition results without renewal.
AI.conclusion: The recovery hypothesis is not established; incomplete references, binding failures, and sequential waits define operational limits. Because the retrospective oracle check matches renewal and also supplies calibration, renewal provides no demonstrated incremental numerical-correctness utility.

title: Implementing rapid reset of superconducting qubits with on-chip dissipation
summary: Rapid and high-fidelity qubit reset is essential for quantum state initialization and quantum error correction. Conventional reset protocols for superconducting qubits often rely on dissipative elements connected to external circuitry, exposing qubits to thermal noise from higher-temperature environments. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a scalable approach to qubit reset and leakage removal over multiple transmon qubits using dedicated dissipation units comprising resonators coupled to on-chip resistive loads. This architecture provides Purcell protection while isolating the qubits from warmer external circuitry. We achieve a median reset time constant of approximately 48 ns for the $|g\rangle-|e\rangle$ transition, with an effective bath temperature of 30 mK. A 400-ns reset pulse yields residual excited-state populations of $0.29\%$ and $0.67\%$ for qubits initialized in $|g\rangle$ and $|e\rangle$, respectively. We further demonstrate efficient leakage removal from the $|f\rangle$ state, reducing its residual population to $0.51\%$. These results establish a simple, reproducible, and easy-to-integrate approach to dissipation engineering in superconducting quantum processors.

AI.tldr: The authors experimentally demonstrate a scalable on-chip qubit reset and leakage-removal scheme for multiple transmons using dedicated dissipation units (resonators coupled to on-chip resistive loads), achieving ~48 ns median reset time, 30 mK effective bath temperature, and sub-1% residual populations.
AI.motivation: Fast, high-fidelity qubit reset is necessary for quantum state initialization and quantum error correction. Conventional superconducting-qubit reset protocols depend on dissipative elements tied to external circuitry, which exposes qubits to thermal noise from warmer environments. The work aims to provide a scalable reset/leakage-removal approach that avoids this thermal exposure while retaining Purcell protection.
AI.method: Dedicated dissipation units consisting of resonators coupled to on-chip resistive loads are integrated with multiple transmon qubits. This architecture isolates qubits from warmer external circuitry and provides Purcell protection. Reset performance is characterized via reset time constants for the |g>-|e> transition and effective bath temperature; a 400-ns reset pulse is used to measure residual excited-state populations, and leakage removal from the |f> state is evaluated.
AI.result: A median reset time constant of ~48 ns is achieved for the |g>-|e> transition with an effective bath temperature of 30 mK. A 400-ns reset pulse yields residual excited-state populations of 0.29% and 0.67% for qubits initialized in |g> and |e>, respectively. Leakage removal from |f> reduces its residual population to 0.51%.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a simple, reproducible, and easily integrable approach to dissipation engineering in superconducting quantum processors, enabling scalable, thermally isolated qubit reset and leakage suppression.

title: Simulating closed- and open-system dynamics of Tavis--Cummings lattices on fault-tolerant quantum computers
summary: Tavis--Cummings lattices couple cavities containing several emitters and host polaritonic many-body dynamics whose real-time correlations are costly to compute classically in two dimensions, especially when unequal emitter relaxation or dephasing rates break permutation symmetry. We analyze logical resources for fault-tolerant closed- and open-system simulation of an atom-resolved lattice with $L$ cavities, $N$ emitters per cavity, and photon cutoff $n\_{\max}$, including target observable estimation. Building on ladder-operator block encoding, we construct circuits for photon hopping and local light--matter exchange and combine them to encode the lattice Hamiltonian. By updating source and destination photon occupations in place, the hopping circuit eliminates the auxiliary $L\lceil\log_2(n\_{\max}+1)\rceil$-qubit photon register used by two-register implementations. Across three uniform-coefficient examples with $16$ to $256$ cavities, the controlled walk uses $4.75$--$8.11%$ fewer Toffoli gates than the paired two-register implementation under matched shared preparation, precision, control, and workspace conventions. For closed systems, we implement real-time evolution with generalized quantum signal processing and bound the cost of estimating retarded cavity spectral functions. For open systems with photon loss, emitter relaxation, and dephasing, we use a sampled first-order dilation and bound the runs and timesteps needed to estimate transient photon statistics such as $g^{(2)}(0)$. With state-preparation and measurement costs explicit, these estimates provide a reference for assessing fault-tolerant light--matter lattice simulation costs.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes logical (fault-tolerant) resource costs for simulating atom-resolved Tavis–Cummings lattices. It designs block-encoded circuits for photon hopping and light–matter exchange that update photon occupations in place, eliminating a separate L·⌈log₂(n_max+1)⌉-qubit register, and uses generalized quantum signal processing (closed systems) and a sampled first-order dilation (open systems) to bound observable-estimation costs.
AI.motivation: Real-time correlations of polaritonic many-body dynamics in 2D Tavis–Cummings lattices are classically expensive, particularly when unequal emitter relaxation or dephasing rates break permutation symmetry, so fault-tolerant quantum simulation cost estimates are needed as a practical reference.
AI.method: Builds on ladder-operator block encoding to construct circuits for photon hopping and local light–matter exchange, combined into a lattice Hamiltonian encoding. The hopping circuit updates source/destination photon occupations in place, removing the auxiliary photon register of two-register implementations. Closed-system real-time evolution uses generalized quantum signal processing with bounds on retarded cavity spectral function estimation; open systems with photon loss, emitter relaxation and dephasing use a sampled first-order dilation with bounds on runs/timesteps for transient photon statistics such as g⁽²⁾(0). State-preparation and measurement costs are made explicit.
AI.result: Across three uniform-coefficient examples with 16–256 cavities, the controlled walk uses 4.75–8.11% fewer Toffoli gates than the paired two-register implementation under matched shared-preparation, precision, control, and workspace conventions.
AI.conclusion: The explicit end-to-end estimates provide a reference for assessing fault-tolerant light–matter lattice simulation costs, including observable estimation with state preparation and measurement accounted for.

authors: Jean-Louis de Bougrenet de la Tocnaye
title: Multidimensional Quantum Block Turbo Codes
summary: The theory of turbo iterative decoding was brought into the quantum coding framework through the development of quantum serial turbo codes and quantum block turbo codes. In this paper, we present a theory for multidimensional quantum block turbo codes, a turbo decoding technique for multi layer product codes. We describe its algorithm and simulate the performance for the 3D case on a depolarizing channel.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a theory of multidimensional quantum block turbo codes, extending turbo iterative decoding to multilayer quantum product codes, and simulates the 3D case over a depolarizing channel.
AI.motivation: Turbo iterative decoding has been imported into quantum coding via quantum serial turbo codes and quantum block turbo codes, but a general theory for multidimensional (multilayer product) quantum turbo codes was lacking.
AI.method: Constructs a theoretical framework for multidimensional quantum block turbo codes, i.e., turbo decoding for multilayer product codes, specifying the decoding algorithm, then evaluates performance by simulating the 3D case on a depolarizing channel.
AI.result: A decoding algorithm for multidimensional quantum block turbo codes is described and simulation results for the 3D case on a depolarizing channel are reported.
AI.conclusion: Turbo iterative decoding generalizes to multidimensional quantum block turbo codes, providing a framework for multilayer product codes with demonstrated 3D performance on the depolarizing channel.

title: The energetic cost of loading classical data in quantum computers
summary: Quantum algorithms for machine learning, chemistry, and cryptanalysis often assume coherent access to classical data at negligible physical cost. We instead treat data loading as a hardware process and quantify the dynamic energetic cost of a quantum random access memory (QRAM) query on a superconducting processor. Using the metric-noise-resource framework, we relate query fidelity and power to gate duration, relative two-qubit drive strength, and the distribution of attenuation across a multi-stage refrigerator, while accounting for thermal photons and gate errors. We analyze the linear-depth multiplexer and the noise-resilient bucket-brigade architectures, adapting the latter to a native superconducting gate set and refining its fidelity analysis using the fully decomposed gate schedule. For a representative bucket-brigade QRAM query with a $12$-qubit address register we obtain a query fidelity of $0.969$. The query consumes $3.51\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{J}$ of dynamic energy, corresponding to an average dynamic power of $4.38\,\mathrm{W}$ and a peak of $64.4\,\mathrm{W}$. Our optimization shows that, at fixed target fidelity, the operating point and attenuation profile can change the average power by a factor of two or more.

AI.tldr: Treating data loading as a hardware process, this work quantifies the dynamic energetic cost of a QRAM query on a superconducting processor, finding fidelities near 0.97 with substantial power requirements whose optimization can vary average power by 2x or more.
AI.motivation: Quantum algorithms assume coherent, negligible-cost classical data access, but this ignores the real hardware cost of data loading. The paper aims to quantify the actual dynamic energy and power cost of a QRAM query on superconducting hardware rather than treating data access as free.
AI.method: Using the metric-noise-resource framework, the authors relate query fidelity and power to gate duration, relative two-qubit drive strength, and attenuation distribution across a multi-stage refrigerator, accounting for thermal photons and gate errors. They analyze both the linear-depth multiplexer and the noise-resilient bucket-brigade architecture, adapting the latter to a native superconducting gate set and refining fidelity analysis via a fully decomposed gate schedule.
AI.result: For a representative bucket-brigade QRAM query with a 12-qubit address register, they obtain a query fidelity of 0.969, consuming 3.51e-4 J of dynamic energy—an average dynamic power of 4.38 W and a peak of 64.4 W. Optimization shows the operating point and attenuation profile can change average power by a factor of two or more at fixed target fidelity.
AI.conclusion: Data loading in quantum algorithms carries non-negligible energetic costs on superconducting hardware. At fixed fidelity, power consumption is highly sensitive to operating point and attenuation profile, implying significant room for energy optimization in QRAM design.

title: Quantum Thermal Transistor via Nonlinear Environmental Coupling
summary: Thermal amplification enables sensitive control of heat currents, providing a basis for heat management and thermal signal processing in quantum devices. For a harmonic oscillator coupled to emitter, collector, and base thermal reservoirs, we recover the absence of thermal amplification when system-reservoir interactions permit only single-quantum exchange. A controlled weak-nonlinearity expansion, supported by numerical stationary solutions, shows that two-quantum exchange at the emitter enables amplification and predicts its onset. When two-quantum exchange dominates at the emitter and collector, varying the base temperature redistributes populations between even and odd oscillator sectors. This changes the emitter and collector heat currents far more than the base current, enabling large thermal amplification. We propose a realization using a longitudinally coupled auxiliary two-level system and bath spectral filtering, specifying conditions for its elimination to yield the required oscillator dynamics. These results establish nonlinear system-reservoir coupling as a resource for controlling heat flow and enabling thermal amplification.

AI.tldr: Thermal amplification is shown to arise in a harmonic oscillator coupled to three thermal reservoirs only when two-quantum exchange is permitted at the emitter, and is strongly enhanced when two-quantum exchange dominates at both emitter and collector.
AI.motivation: Thermal amplification would enable sensitive control of heat currents for heat management and thermal signal processing in quantum devices, but it is known to be absent under the standard single-quantum (weak-coupling) system-reservoir exchange. The paper asks what microscopic ingredient is required to recover amplification.
AI.method: The authors study a harmonic oscillator coupled to emitter, collector, and base reservoirs. They use a controlled weak-nonlinearity expansion, corroborated by numerical stationary solutions, to analyze multi-quantum exchange channels. They then examine the case where two-quantum exchange dominates at emitter and collector and vary the base temperature. A physical realization is proposed using a longitudinally coupled auxiliary two-level system plus bath spectral filtering.
AI.result: With only single-quantum exchange, thermal amplification is absent. Two-quantum exchange at the emitter enables amplification, and the expansion predicts its onset. When two-quantum exchange dominates at emitter and collector, changing the base temperature redistributes populations between even and odd oscillator sectors, altering emitter and collector currents far more than the base current, yielding large amplification.
AI.conclusion: Nonlinear system-reservoir coupling is identified as a resource for controlling heat flow and enabling thermal amplification. The proposed auxiliary two-level system with spectral filtering provides a concrete platform, with conditions specified for eliminating the auxiliary to recover the required oscillator dynamics.

title: Finite-Key Readiness and Authentication-Key Replenishment in QKD-Assisted UAV Edge Computing
summary: A service that needs fresh quantum keys must wait for key release, and may be denied it, before protected computation starts. We quantify this cost for a trusted stationary UAV serving two ground gateways, each obtaining its keys from one finite-key decoy-state BB84 attempt with parameters fixed in advance. A count-level Monte Carlo model, reproduced by a semi-analytic model, links key acceptance to protected upload, computation, and download, including failed attempts and hover energy. At 26~dB effective optical loss, with authentication hashing at its proxy-benchmarked, near-zero cost, fresh keys raise the 95th-percentile completion time of both tasks from 10.37 to 28.65~s; hover energy grows in proportion. The scalar rate models evaluated here miss the deadline limit on the block size. The pulse budget lies in a window bounded below by authentication-key replenishment and above by the deadline; for a fixed source, channel, and acceptance model, the authentication debit shifts the floor, whereas hashing cost does not. At a 35-s deadline the largest tested loss with a non-empty window is 27~dB at 1\% misalignment and 22~dB at 2\%; at 3\% no tested setting has one. Conditional on the assumed acquisition probability, the selected configurations meet this deadline with simultaneous lower confidence bounds of 96.9--97.3\% on held-out trials, at 26~dB and at 18--20~dB with 2\% misalignment. A high-cost stress reference that charges hashing in full narrows the window and lowers these loss limits to 26 and 20~dB at the reference processing capacity. A small rise in error rate or loss pushes the deadline probability well below its target and drains authentication keys, while the protocol's security parameter is unchanged.

AI.tldr: Fresh quantum keys gate protected UAV computation: at 26 dB loss, key release raises 95th-percentile completion from 10.37 to 28.65 s, and feasible pulse-budget windows are bounded by authentication-key replenishment below and the deadline above.
AI.motivation: Services requiring fresh quantum keys must wait for—and may be denied—key release before protected computation can begin; the paper aims to quantify this latency and acceptance cost for a stationary UAV serving two ground gateways via finite-key decoy-state BB84.
AI.method: Each gateway obtains keys from a single finite-key decoy-state BB84 attempt with pre-fixed parameters. A count-level Monte Carlo model, cross-validated by a semi-analytic model, links key acceptance to protected upload, computation, and download, accounting for failed attempts and hover energy. Scalar rate models and a high-cost hashing stress reference are also evaluated.
AI.result: At 26 dB effective optical loss and near-zero authentication hashing cost, fresh keys raise 95th-percentile completion time of both tasks from 10.37 s to 28.65 s, with hover energy growing proportionally. Scalar rate models miss the deadline-induced block-size limit. The pulse budget window is bounded below by authentication-key replenishment and above by the deadline; authentication debit shifts the floor, hashing cost does not. At a 35 s deadline, the largest loss with a non-empty window is 27 dB at 1% misalignment and 22 dB at 2%; none exists at 3%. Conditional on acquisition probability, selected configurations meet the deadline with simultaneous lower confidence bounds of 96.9–97.3% on held-out trials at 26 dB and 18–20 dB with 2% misalignment. Full hashing charges narrow the window, lowering loss limits to 26 and 20 dB. Small increases in error rate or loss drive deadline probability far below target and deplete authentication keys while the security parameter remains unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Fresh-key gating is a dominant and quantifiable cost in key-assisted UAV computation. Feasibility is governed by a narrow pulse-budget window jointly constrained by authentication-key replenishment and task deadlines, and is highly sensitive to error rate and loss even at fixed security parameter—so scalar rate models are inadequate for deadline-aware design.

title: Nonperturbative string dynamics in a (2+1)D lattice gauge theory on a superconducting quantum processor
summary: Electric flux strings underpin confinement in gauge theories. In two spatial dimensions, their evolution involves competing processes of charge motion, pair creation, and transverse deformation. Accessing these dynamics beyond perturbative limits challenges classical approaches, as entanglement growth restricts the times accessible to tensor-network simulations. Here we use quantum simulation to investigate a (2+1)D Z2 lattice gauge theory with dynamical matter and an explicit magnetic plaquette interaction, spanning strongly confined and nonperturbative deconfined regimes. Using 63 superconducting qubits, including 12 ancillas, we evolve initially localized strings with static or dynamical endpoint charges. Spatially resolved measurements reveal rapid charge and flux spreading in the deconfined regime, enhanced matter occupation in the string interior near the pair-creation resonance, and suppressed spreading at strong electric fields. String-path occupations further probe transverse rearrangements between configurations connected by plaquette operations. Retaining separate matter and gauge degrees of freedom makes local Gauss-law constraints directly accessible for error detection. Combining these constraints with ancilla checks and noise rescaling, we measure dynamics in circuits containing up to 15 second-order Trotter steps. Our results establish quantum simulation as a practical approach to exploring nonperturbative string dynamics in two spatial dimensions, with gauge redundancy serving as an experimental resource.

AI.tldr: Using 63 superconducting qubits (12 ancillas), the authors quantum-simulate a (2+1)D Z2 lattice gauge theory with dynamical matter and a magnetic plaquette term, tracking the real-time evolution of electric flux strings across confined and deconfined regimes.
AI.motivation: Electric flux strings are central to confinement in gauge theories, but their (2+1)D dynamics—charge motion, pair creation, and transverse string deformation—defy perturbative and classical treatment because entanglement growth limits tensor-network reach. The authors aim to access these nonperturbative string dynamics directly via quantum simulation.
AI.method: A (2+1)D Z2 lattice gauge theory with dynamical matter and an explicit magnetic plaquette interaction is encoded on 63 superconducting qubits (including 12 ancillas), keeping matter and gauge degrees of freedom separate. Initially localized strings with static or dynamical endpoint charges are evolved using second-order Trotter circuits (up to 15 steps). Local Gauss-law constraints, ancilla checks, and noise rescaling are used for error detection and mitigation; spatially resolved measurements track charge/flux spreading and string-path occupations.
AI.result: Spatially resolved measurements show rapid charge and flux spreading in the deconfined regime, enhanced matter occupation in the string interior near the pair-creation resonance, and suppressed spreading at strong electric fields. String-path occupations reveal transverse rearrangements between configurations linked by plaquette operations.
AI.conclusion: Quantum simulation is a practical route to probing nonperturbative string dynamics in two spatial dimensions, and gauge redundancy—retained via separate matter and gauge registers—serves as a useful experimental resource for error detection rather than a liability.
